title: A&P: Neuro & Musculoskeletal
summary: How nerves signal, how the brain is wired and supplied, and how bones, joints and muscles are built and broken. Taught from zero with the mechanism first, then the bedside finding it produces.

lessons.title: The neuron, the signal and the synapse
lessons.body:
## A battery that fires

A neuron has three working parts: **dendrites** that collect incoming signals, a **cell body (soma)** that adds them up, and a single **axon** that carries the decision away to the next cell.

At rest, the inside of a neuron sits at about `-70 mV` relative to the outside. That charge separation is built and held by the sodium-potassium ATPase, which pumps three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in, burning ATP the whole time. Roughly `20%` of the body's oxygen use goes to the brain largely to keep these pumps running, which is why neurons die within minutes of losing blood flow: no ATP means no gradient, and no gradient means no signal.

When enough incoming signal arrives to push the membrane from `-70` up to the threshold near `-55 mV`, voltage-gated sodium channels snap open. Sodium floods in, the inside swings positive to about `+30 mV`, and that is the **action potential**. It is all-or-none: reaching threshold produces a full-size spike every time, and falling short produces nothing. Then sodium channels close, potassium channels open, potassium leaves, and the cell repolarizes, usually overshooting slightly (hyperpolarization) before settling back.

During the **refractory period** the cell cannot fire again, which is what forces the signal to travel in one direction instead of echoing backward.

### Myelin and speed

Most axons are wrapped in **myelin**, a fatty insulator laid down by oligodendrocytes in the brain and cord and by Schwann cells in the peripheral nerves. Gaps between wraps, the **nodes of Ranvier**, are the only places ion channels are exposed, so the impulse jumps node to node instead of crawling along the whole membrane. That jumping (saltatory conduction) is the difference between about `0.5 to 2 meters per second` in a small unmyelinated fiber and up to `120 meters per second` in a large myelinated one.

Strip the myelin and conduction slows or fails. That is multiple sclerosis in the central nervous system and Guillain-Barre syndrome in the peripheral nerves, which is why Guillain-Barre climbs from the feet upward and can reach the diaphragm.

### The synapse

Axons do not touch the next cell. The signal reaches the axon terminal, calcium enters, vesicles fuse with the membrane and dump **neurotransmitter** into a gap about `20 to 40 nanometers` wide, and those molecules bind receptors on the next cell. The signal is then ended by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion. Nearly every psychiatric and many neurologic drugs work by changing one of those three exits.

Six transmitters carry most of the clinical weight.

| Transmitter | Main job | A drug that targets it |
|---|---|---|
| Acetylcholine | Muscle activation at the neuromuscular junction; parasympathetic effects | Atropine blocks its muscarinic receptors |
| Norepinephrine | Sympathetic arousal, alertness, vascular tone | Norepinephrine infusion; SNRIs block reuptake |
| Dopamine | Movement, reward, motivation | Levodopa replaces it in Parkinson's; haloperidol blocks it |
| Serotonin | Mood, sleep, appetite, gut motility | SSRIs such as sertraline block reuptake |
| GABA | The main inhibitory brake | Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam enhance it |
| Glutamate | The main excitatory accelerator | Ketamine blocks its NMDA receptor |

Two of those deserve a note. GABA and glutamate are the volume controls for the entire brain: glutamate turns activity up, GABA turns it down, and a seizure is essentially that balance tipping toward glutamate. **Endorphins** are the body's own opioids, binding the same mu receptors as morphine and fentanyl, which is why naloxone reverses both.

> **Key:** An action potential is all-or-none. Strength is coded by how often the neuron fires and how many neurons fire, never by how big each spike is.

> **On shift:** When a benzodiazepine stops a seizure, it is not sedating the patient into submission. It is enhancing GABA, the brake, against runaway glutamate excitation.
keyPoints: Resting potential is about -70 mV, threshold about -55 mV, peak about +30 mV, maintained by the sodium-potassium ATPase
Action potentials are all-or-none; intensity is coded by firing frequency, not spike size
Myelin plus nodes of Ranvier allow saltatory conduction up to about 120 m/s; demyelination causes MS and Guillain-Barre
Signals cross synapses chemically and are ended by reuptake, enzyme breakdown or diffusion
GABA is the brake and glutamate the accelerator; acetylcholine, norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin each have named drugs

checks.q: Why does brain tissue die within minutes of losing blood flow?
choices: Myelin dissolves immediately without oxygen
Without ATP the sodium-potassium pump stops, the ion gradient collapses, and no signal is possible
Neurotransmitters are washed out of the synapse
Neurons rupture from osmotic pressure within seconds
checks.why: The resting potential is an actively maintained gradient that costs continuous ATP. Neurons have almost no energy reserve, so when perfusion stops the pump stops, the gradient dissipates, and irreversible injury follows quickly. Myelin loss and transmitter washout are far slower processes.

checks.q: A patient has ascending weakness starting in the feet after a diarrheal illness. Nerve studies show slowed conduction. What is the mechanism?
choices: Loss of dopamine in the basal ganglia
Excess glutamate at NMDA receptors
Demyelination of peripheral nerves, slowing saltatory conduction
Failure of the sodium-potassium ATPase in muscle
checks.why: This is Guillain-Barre syndrome. Stripping myelin removes the insulation that lets impulses jump node to node, so conduction slows and eventually fails. The danger is ascent to the diaphragm, so serial vital capacity is monitored.

checks.q: Which pair correctly matches a transmitter to a drug that targets it?
choices: GABA and lorazepam
Dopamine and atropine
Acetylcholine and levodopa
Serotonin and naloxone
checks.why: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA, the main inhibitory transmitter. Atropine blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, levodopa replaces dopamine, and naloxone blocks opioid receptors where endorphins act.

lessons.title: How the brain is organized, and what each part costs when it fails
lessons.body:
## Four lobes, four jobs

The cerebral cortex is split into two hemispheres, each with four lobes, and each lobe announces itself when it is injured.

**Frontal lobe.** Voluntary movement from the primary motor strip (precentral gyrus), plus judgment, planning, personality and impulse control. Broca's area, in the dominant frontal lobe, produces speech. Damage gives contralateral weakness, or an expressive aphasia where the patient knows what they want to say and cannot get the words out, or a personality change that families notice long before any doctor does.

**Parietal lobe.** Sensation from the primary sensory strip (postcentral gyrus), plus spatial awareness. Damage on the non-dominant side produces **neglect**, where a patient will genuinely not acknowledge one side of the world, including their own arm.

**Temporal lobe.** Hearing, memory formation through the hippocampus, and Wernicke's area for language comprehension. A Wernicke's aphasia is fluent but meaningless speech in a patient who does not realize anything is wrong.

**Occipital lobe.** Vision. An occipital stroke takes visual fields, not strength, so patients may arrive complaining only that they cannot see to one side.

Dominance matters. In roughly `95%` of right-handed people and about `70%` of left-handed people, language lives in the left hemisphere. So a left-hemisphere stroke tends to produce aphasia and a right-hemisphere stroke tends to produce neglect.

### Below the cortex

**Basal ganglia** sit deep in the hemispheres and smooth voluntary movement. When dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra die, the output goes wrong and you get Parkinson's disease: resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability. Replacing dopamine with levodopa treats it; blocking dopamine with antipsychotics can produce a drug-induced version of it.

**Thalamus** is the relay station. Almost every sensory pathway except smell synapses there before reaching the cortex.

**Hypothalamus** is the thermostat and the hormone controller: temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythm, and the pituitary above all else.

**Cerebellum** sits at the back under the occipital lobe and coordinates movement without initiating any of it. Cerebellar damage gives ataxia, an unsteady wide-based gait, intention tremor that worsens as the hand approaches the target, and dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing. Crucially, cerebellar signs are **ipsilateral**, on the same side as the lesion, unlike almost everything else in the brain.

**Brainstem** is midbrain, pons and medulla, and it is where the non-negotiables live: the medulla runs breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, and the pons helps modulate breathing. Cranial nerves III through XII emerge here. A brainstem stroke can therefore produce crossed findings, such as cranial nerve loss on one side with limb weakness on the other.

### Being awake versus making sense

Consciousness has two parts. **Arousal**, being awake at all, is generated by the **reticular activating system (RAS)**, a mesh of neurons running through the brainstem up into the thalamus. **Content**, making sense, requires the cortex. So a patient can be awake and completely incoherent, or fully intact and unable to wake up.

That gives a practical rule for altered mental status. A **structural** cause (bleed, mass, herniation, stroke) presses on the RAS or on one side of the cortex, so it tends to produce **focal** findings and unequal pupils. A **metabolic or toxic** cause (low glucose, sodium, oxygen, sepsis, liver or kidney failure, drugs) affects the whole brain at once, so findings are **symmetric** and pupils are usually equal and reactive.

Three states get confused with each other. **Delirium** is acute, fluctuates hour to hour, impairs attention first, and is caused by something medical that can be fixed. **Dementia** is chronic, progresses over months to years, and impairs memory while attention stays intact until late. **Psychosis** leaves orientation and attention intact but distorts content, and it rarely begins for the first time after age `40`.

> **Key:** Cortical and motor findings are contralateral. Cerebellar findings are ipsilateral. Brainstem lesions can be both at once.

> **Trap:** A fluctuating, inattentive elderly patient is delirious until proven otherwise, and delirium means go find the cause. Writing it off as dementia misses the infection, the drug or the sodium.
keyPoints: Frontal: movement, judgment, Broca's expressive aphasia; parietal: sensation and non-dominant neglect
Temporal: memory and Wernicke's fluent aphasia; occipital: vision only
Basal ganglia and dopamine loss give Parkinson's; cerebellum gives ipsilateral ataxia and intention tremor
The RAS in the brainstem provides arousal; the cortex provides content
Structural causes of altered mental status are focal and asymmetric; metabolic causes are global and symmetric

checks.q: A patient speaks fluently but the sentences are nonsense, and he does not appear aware of the problem. Where is the lesion?
choices: Dominant frontal lobe, Broca's area
Dominant temporal lobe, Wernicke's area
Cerebellum
Occipital lobe
checks.why: Wernicke's area handles comprehension, so damage there leaves speech fluent but empty, and the patient usually lacks insight. Broca's aphasia is the opposite: effortful, sparse speech with preserved understanding and obvious frustration.

checks.q: Which finding is ipsilateral to the lesion rather than contralateral?
choices: Arm weakness from a motor strip infarct
Sensory loss from a parietal infarct
Visual field loss from an occipital infarct
Limb ataxia from a cerebellar infarct
checks.why: Cerebellar hemispheres control the same side of the body, so a left cerebellar lesion causes left-sided ataxia and dysmetria. Motor and sensory cortex findings cross, and occipital lesions affect contralateral visual fields.

checks.q: An 82-year-old is newly confused, fluctuating through the day, and cannot sustain attention. Pupils are equal, no focal weakness. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: Delirium from a metabolic or toxic cause; go looking for it
Dementia, so arrange outpatient follow-up
New-onset psychosis
A structural lesion pressing on the reticular activating system
checks.why: Acute onset, fluctuation and impaired attention define delirium, and symmetric findings with reactive pupils point at a global metabolic or toxic cause such as infection, glucose, sodium or a drug. Dementia is chronic and progressive, and first-episode psychosis after 40 is rare.

lessons.title: Meninges, bleeds, CSF and pressure inside a closed box
lessons.body:
## Three wrappers, three spaces to bleed into

The brain is wrapped in three membranes. Outermost is the **dura mater**, a tough leather-like layer stuck to the inside of the skull. Beneath it is the fine **arachnoid mater**, and beneath that the **pia mater**, a delicate film glued to the brain surface itself. The names of the hemorrhages are just the space the blood found.

**Epidural hematoma.** Between skull and dura, almost always **arterial**, classically the middle meningeal artery torn by a temporal bone fracture. Arterial pressure fills it fast. The textbook story is a blow to the head, brief unconsciousness, a **lucid interval** of minutes to hours, then rapid deterioration. On CT it is a **convex lens shape** that does not cross suture lines, because the dura is anchored there.

**Subdural hematoma.** Between dura and arachnoid, from torn **bridging veins**. Venous pressure is low, so it fills slowly. It is the bleed of the elderly and of heavy drinkers, whose brain atrophy stretches those veins, presenting over days to weeks with headache, confusion or personality change after a fall nobody remembers. On CT it is **crescent shaped** and does cross sutures.

**Subarachnoid hemorrhage.** Between arachnoid and pia, where the CSF lives, usually a ruptured berry aneurysm. The hallmark is **sudden worst-ever headache at maximal intensity within seconds**, often with neck stiffness, vomiting and photophobia from meningeal irritation. CT within `6 hours` is highly sensitive; after that, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia.

### CSF and the flow that can block

CSF is made by the **choroid plexus** at roughly `500 mL per day`, while only about `150 mL` is present at once, so the whole volume turns over about three times daily. It cushions the brain, removes waste and supports its weight.

The path: lateral ventricles, foramen of Monro, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, out into the subarachnoid space, and reabsorbed into venous blood through the arachnoid granulations.

Block that path and pressure rises upstream: **obstructive hydrocephalus**. Fail to reabsorb, as when subarachnoid blood clogs the granulations, and you get **communicating hydrocephalus**. In an infant the unfused skull simply enlarges and the fontanelle bulges; in an adult the skull cannot give, so pressure climbs.

The **blood-brain barrier** is tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells wrapped by astrocyte foot processes. It excludes most large molecules and many drugs, which is why levodopa is used instead of dopamine, which cannot cross. Inflammation loosens it, which is why some antibiotics penetrate better in meningitis than in a healthy brain.

### The skull is a fixed box

The **Monro-Kellie doctrine** says the skull's volume is constant and contains only three things: brain tissue (about `80%`), blood (about `10%`) and CSF (about `10%`). Add a fourth thing, such as a hematoma or swelling, and one of the three must be displaced or pressure rises.

That displacement is why compensation works for a while and then stops abruptly. CSF is pushed out first, then venous blood. Once both are gone, small further increases in volume cause steep rises in pressure.

Normal **intracranial pressure (ICP)** is `5` to `15 mmHg`, and treatment is usually triggered above `20 to 22 mmHg`. What actually matters is what is left over for perfusion: **cerebral perfusion pressure `CPP = MAP - ICP`**, with a target generally above `60 mmHg`. Read that equation twice. Hypotension is as damaging as intracranial hypertension, because both shrink the difference.

**Cushing's triad** is the late warning that the brainstem is being squeezed: **rising systolic pressure with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular breathing**. It is the body raising MAP to preserve CPP, with the bradycardia arriving as a baroreflex answer to that pressure. Cushing's triad is not a sign you have time.

Herniation is brain tissue being forced where it does not belong. **Uncal herniation** pushes the medial temporal lobe over the tentorium onto cranial nerve III, giving a fixed, dilated pupil on the **same side** as the lesion with weakness on the opposite side. **Tonsillar herniation** forces the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum onto the medulla, which stops breathing and circulation.

Hyperventilation drops PaCO2, which constricts cerebral vessels, which lowers blood volume and therefore ICP within minutes. It also reduces cerebral blood flow, so it is a **bridge measure only** for signs of active herniation, targeting an EtCO2 around `30 to 35 mmHg`, never a routine therapy.

> **Key:** `CPP = MAP - ICP`. Protecting the brain means both lowering ICP and refusing to let the blood pressure fall.

> **Trap:** The lucid interval belongs to the epidural bleed and appears in maybe a third of cases. Its absence proves nothing.
keyPoints: Epidural: arterial, middle meningeal, lucid interval, convex lens on CT, does not cross sutures
Subdural: bridging veins, slow, elderly and alcohol use, crescent shape, crosses sutures
Subarachnoid: thunderclap worst-ever headache, CT within 6 hours then LP for xanthochromia
Monro-Kellie: brain, blood and CSF in a fixed box, so compensation ends abruptly; normal ICP 5 to 15 mmHg
CPP = MAP - ICP with a target above 60; Cushing's triad is hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing

checks.q: A 19-year-old is struck in the temple, is briefly unconscious, wakes and talks normally for 40 minutes, then rapidly becomes unresponsive with a dilated right pupil. Which bleed and which vessel?
choices: Subdural hematoma from bridging veins
Epidural hematoma from the middle meningeal artery
Subarachnoid hemorrhage from a berry aneurysm
Intraparenchymal hemorrhage from hypertension
checks.why: The lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration is the classic epidural pattern, because arterial bleeding fills the epidural space quickly. The dilated pupil is uncal herniation compressing cranial nerve III on the same side as the lesion. Subdural bleeding is venous and much slower.

checks.q: A head-injured patient has ICP 28 mmHg and MAP 70 mmHg. What is the cerebral perfusion pressure and why does it matter?
choices: 98 mmHg, which is adequate
28 mmHg, which is the number to treat
42 mmHg, which is below the target of about 60
70 mmHg, because MAP is what perfuses the brain
checks.why: CPP = MAP - ICP = 70 - 28 = 42 mmHg, well under the usual target above 60. Raising CPP means lowering ICP, supporting MAP, or both. Reading MAP alone ignores the pressure the brain is being squeezed by.

checks.q: Which set of findings is Cushing's triad?
choices: Hypotension, tachycardia and rapid breathing
Rising systolic pressure with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing
Fever, neck stiffness and photophobia
Fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness and a lucid interval
checks.why: Cushing's triad is the late brainstem response to critically high ICP: the body raises MAP to preserve CPP, the baroreflex answers with bradycardia, and the damaged medulla breathes irregularly. Choice 1 is shock, choice 3 is meningeal irritation, and choice 4 describes uncal herniation and epidural bleeding.

lessons.title: Brain circulation and stroke syndromes
lessons.body:
## Two front doors, two back doors, one ring

The brain gets `15` to `20%` of cardiac output and has essentially no stored fuel, so it depends entirely on continuous flow. Blood arrives by four vessels.

The **anterior circulation** comes from the two **internal carotid arteries**, each dividing into the **middle cerebral artery (MCA)** and the **anterior cerebral artery (ACA)**. The **posterior circulation** comes from the two **vertebral arteries**, which join to form the single **basilar artery**, which supplies the brainstem and cerebellum and then splits into the two **posterior cerebral arteries (PCA)**.

Those systems are joined at the base of the brain by the **Circle of Willis**, connected by the anterior communicating artery in front and the two posterior communicating arteries behind. The ring is a backup route: if one vessel is slowly occluded, flow can cross over. It is complete in only about `20 to 50%` of people, which is part of why identical occlusions produce different deficits in different patients. It is also where berry aneurysms form, most often at the anterior communicating artery.

### Reading the deficit backward to the vessel

The motor and sensory strips are mapped like a distorted body (the homunculus), with the face and hand occupying a huge area on the lateral surface and the leg tucked over the top edge into the midline. That geography is the whole trick.

| Vessel | Territory | Classic deficit |
|---|---|---|
| MCA | Lateral hemisphere: face and arm motor and sensory, language, spatial attention | Contralateral face and arm weakness worse than leg, plus aphasia if dominant or neglect if non-dominant, and gaze deviation toward the lesion |
| ACA | Medial surface, the leg area | Contralateral leg weakness worse than arm, sometimes urinary incontinence and abulia |
| PCA | Occipital lobe and thalamus | Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with preserved strength |
| Vertebrobasilar | Brainstem and cerebellum | The Ds: dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, plus ataxia and crossed findings |

The **MCA syndrome** is the one to know cold, because MCA territory strokes are the most common. Contralateral weakness and numbness of the face and arm with a relatively spared leg, aphasia when the dominant (usually left) hemisphere is involved, neglect when the non-dominant side is, and the eyes drifting toward the side of the lesion.

Posterior circulation strokes are the ones that get missed, because dizziness, nausea and unsteadiness look like a vestibular problem. The tell is company: dizziness **plus** double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, or an inability to sit unsupported is a posterior stroke until proven otherwise.

### The penumbra and the clock

An occluded artery produces two zones. The **core** is tissue already dead, where flow has fallen below roughly `10 mL per 100 g per minute`. Around it is the **penumbra**, tissue that has lost enough flow to stop working but not enough to die yet, kept marginally alive by collateral vessels. The penumbra is silent electrically but salvageable, and it is the entire target of stroke treatment. Untreated, it is consumed by the core, at an often-quoted rate of roughly `1.9 million` neurons per minute.

That is why the first question asked about every stroke patient is **last known well**, not "when did you notice." It means the last moment the patient was seen at their baseline, because a deficit found on waking has been developing for an unknown time. Treatment windows are measured from that moment: thrombolytics generally within `4.5 hours`, and mechanical thrombectomy for a large vessel occlusion out to `24 hours` in selected patients whose imaging still shows salvageable penumbra.

A **transient ischemic attack (TIA)** is the same event that resolved, now defined by the absence of infarction on imaging rather than by a time limit. It is not reassurance. Stroke risk after a TIA is highest in the first `48 hours`.

> **Key:** Face and arm worse than leg means MCA. Leg worse than arm means ACA. Vision alone means PCA. Dizziness with other Ds means posterior circulation.

> **On shift:** Get last known well as a clock time from a named witness, and get a glucose, because hypoglycemia imitates a stroke perfectly and is fixable in seconds.
keyPoints: Anterior circulation is carotid to MCA and ACA; posterior is vertebral to basilar to PCA
The Circle of Willis is a collateral ring, complete in only 20 to 50% of people, and the site of most berry aneurysms
MCA stroke: contralateral face and arm weakness, aphasia if dominant, neglect if non-dominant
The penumbra is stunned but salvageable tissue, which is why last known well sets the treatment clock
Thrombolysis generally within 4.5 hours, thrombectomy up to 24 hours in selected large vessel occlusions

checks.q: A 68-year-old has right facial droop, right arm weakness, a nearly normal right leg, and cannot produce speech. Which vessel and which hemisphere?
choices: Right ACA
Left MCA
Left PCA
Basilar artery
checks.why: Face and arm weakness out of proportion to leg is MCA territory, and deficits are contralateral, so a right-sided deficit means a left-sided lesion. Aphasia confirms the dominant hemisphere. ACA would spare the arm and hit the leg, and PCA would take visual fields.

checks.q: Why is 'last known well' the critical history point rather than when symptoms were noticed?
choices: It determines which hemisphere is involved
It predicts whether the stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic
Treatment windows are measured from it, and salvageable penumbra shrinks with time
It is required only for documentation and billing
checks.why: The penumbra is stunned tissue that dies progressively, so eligibility for thrombolysis (about 4.5 hours) and thrombectomy (up to 24 hours in selected patients) is measured from the last moment the patient was at baseline. A deficit discovered on waking may already be hours old.

checks.q: Which presentation should raise concern for a posterior circulation stroke rather than a peripheral vertigo?
choices: Isolated spinning sensation worsened by head position
Dizziness with double vision, slurred speech and inability to sit unsupported
Dizziness with unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus
Dizziness with nausea after a viral illness
checks.why: Posterior circulation strokes travel in company: the Ds of dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria and dysphagia plus truncal ataxia. Isolated positional vertigo, or vertigo with hearing symptoms, points at the inner ear rather than the brainstem.

lessons.title: Twelve cranial nerves and the exam that finds them
lessons.body:
## Nerves that skip the spinal cord

Twelve pairs of nerves leave the brain directly. Numbers I and II come off the cerebrum; III through XII emerge from the brainstem, which is why testing them localizes brainstem injury so precisely. Each one is either sensory, motor, or both.

| Nerve | Job | 10-second test | Seen clinically as |
|---|---|---|---|
| I Olfactory | Smell | Ask about smell changes | Lost after head trauma shearing the nerve at the cribriform plate |
| II Optic | Vision, afferent pupil | Visual fields by confrontation, visual acuity | Field cut in PCA stroke; afferent pupil defect in optic neuritis |
| III Oculomotor | Most eye movement, eyelid, pupil constriction | Follow a finger; check pupil size and reaction | Blown pupil with a down-and-out eye in uncal herniation |
| IV Trochlear | Superior oblique, eye down and in | Look down and toward the nose | Vertical diplopia going downstairs |
| V Trigeminal | Face sensation, chewing | Light touch on forehead, cheek, jaw; clench teeth | Trigeminal neuralgia; loss after facial fracture |
| VI Abducens | Lateral rectus, eye outward | Look to the side | Long course makes it the first to fail in raised ICP |
| VII Facial | Facial movement, taste on front of tongue | Raise eyebrows, close eyes tight, smile, puff cheeks | Bell's palsy spares nothing; a stroke spares the forehead |
| VIII Vestibulocochlear | Hearing, balance | Rub fingers by each ear | Hearing loss, vertigo, acoustic neuroma |
| IX Glossopharyngeal | Back of tongue, gag, swallow | Say ahh, look for symmetric palate rise | Aspiration risk after stroke |
| X Vagus | Palate, vocal cords, parasympathetic to organs | Voice quality, gag with IX | Hoarseness, absent gag, bradycardia with stimulation |
| XI Accessory | Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius | Shrug shoulders, turn head against resistance | Shoulder droop after neck surgery |
| XII Hypoglossal | Tongue movement | Stick tongue out and move side to side | Tongue deviates toward the weak side |

### The two highest-yield distinctions

**Bell's palsy versus a stroke.** The forehead muscles receive input from both hemispheres, so a cortical lesion on one side still leaves the forehead working. A peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell's) knocks out the whole half of the face including the forehead and eye closure. Ask the patient to raise both eyebrows. If the forehead wrinkles on the weak side, suspect a stroke, and if it does not, suspect the nerve itself.

**The pupil.** Cranial nerve II carries light in and cranial nerve III carries constriction out. Shine light in one eye and both pupils should constrict (direct and consensual). A pupil that does not constrict to direct light but does constrict when the other eye is lit has an afferent, or optic nerve, problem. A pupil that is large and unreactive in an eye that sees normally has an efferent, or CN III, problem, which in a head-injured patient means herniation until proven otherwise.

### The neurological exam, in the order a PA performs it

The sequence is fixed so that nothing is skipped: **mental status**, then **cranial nerves**, then **motor**, then **sensory**, then **reflexes**, then **coordination**, then **gait**.

Mental status covers level of consciousness, orientation, attention, language and memory. Motor covers bulk, tone, drift and strength graded `0` to `5`. Sensory covers light touch, pain, and position sense. Reflexes are graded `0` to `4+`. Coordination is finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin and rapid alternating movements. Gait is often the most informative single test and the one most often skipped, because walking requires motor, sensory, cerebellar and vestibular systems to work together.

A **focal deficit** means a finding that maps to one specific location in the nervous system: this arm, this visual field, this cranial nerve. Focal points toward a structural lesion, such as a stroke, bleed or mass. Global, symmetric findings point toward a metabolic or toxic cause.

> **Key:** Forehead spared means central (stroke). Forehead involved means peripheral (Bell's palsy).

> **On the exam:** "Down and out" pupil with ptosis is cranial nerve III. Inability to abduct one eye is cranial nerve VI, which fails early and nonspecifically with raised intracranial pressure.
keyPoints: Cranial nerves III through XII emerge from the brainstem, so testing them localizes brainstem injury
Bell's palsy involves the forehead; a cortical stroke spares it because the forehead has bilateral input
CN II carries light in and CN III carries constriction out; a fixed dilated pupil after head injury is herniation
CN VI has the longest course and fails early with raised ICP
Exam order: mental status, cranial nerves, motor, sensory, reflexes, coordination, gait

checks.q: A patient cannot wrinkle the forehead or close the eye on the left, and the left corner of the mouth droops. Where is the lesion?
choices: Right motor cortex, a stroke
The left facial nerve itself, a peripheral palsy
Left cranial nerve V
Left cranial nerve III
checks.why: Forehead involvement means the lesion is in the nerve, not the cortex, because the forehead receives bilateral cortical input and is spared in a central lesion. CN V is facial sensation and chewing, and CN III controls the eyelid and pupil.

checks.q: Which cranial nerve is most likely to fail early and nonspecifically when intracranial pressure rises?
choices: Cranial nerve I
Cranial nerve IV
Cranial nerve VI
Cranial nerve XI
checks.why: The abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course, so it is stretched first as pressure rises, producing an inability to abduct the eye and horizontal double vision. It is a false localizing sign because it does not indicate where the pressure originates.

checks.q: What does a focal deficit tell you?
choices: The findings map to one anatomical location, favoring a structural cause
The patient has a metabolic derangement
The deficit will resolve within 24 hours
The cause is psychiatric rather than neurologic
checks.why: Focal means traceable to a single site, such as one limb, one visual field or one cranial nerve, which points to a structural lesion like stroke, bleed or mass. Metabolic and toxic causes act on the whole brain and produce symmetric, global findings.

lessons.title: The spinal cord: tracts, levels and what an injury costs
lessons.body:
## A cable with named lanes

The cord runs from the brainstem to about `L1` or `L2` in an adult, then continues as a bundle of nerve roots called the **cauda equina**. Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves leave it: `8` cervical, `12` thoracic, `5` lumbar, `5` sacral and `1` coccygeal.

Three tracts carry almost everything you need at recognition level.

**Corticospinal tract** carries voluntary motor commands downward. It crosses in the medulla, so it is already on the opposite side by the time it enters the cord. A cord lesion therefore causes weakness on the **same side** as the lesion, below it.

**Dorsal columns** carry fine touch, vibration and position sense upward, traveling **uncrossed** in the cord and crossing in the medulla. So a cord lesion costs vibration and position sense on the **same side**.

**Spinothalamic tract** carries pain and temperature upward, and it crosses within one or two levels of entering the cord. So a cord lesion costs pain and temperature on the **opposite side**.

That is the whole explanation of **Brown-Sequard syndrome**, a hemisection of the cord: ipsilateral weakness, ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting a level or two below.

### Levels you can use

A **dermatome** is the strip of skin supplied by one nerve root. Six anchors cover most of the body.

| Level | Landmark |
|---|---|
| C4 | Top of the shoulders |
| T4 | Nipple line |
| T10 | Umbilicus |
| L1 | Groin |
| L4 | Kneecap and medial shin |
| S1 | Lateral foot and little toe |

A **myotome** is the muscle group supplied by one root, tested at recognition level: `C5` shoulder abduction, `C6` elbow flexion and wrist extension, `C7` elbow extension, `C8` finger flexion, `T1` finger spread, `L2 to L3` hip flexion, `L4` knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion, `L5` big toe extension, `S1` ankle plantar flexion.

Deep tendon reflexes test a root, a peripheral nerve and the cord segment at once. Biceps is `C5` and `C6`, brachioradialis `C6`, triceps `C7`, patellar `L4`, Achilles `S1`. Grade them `0` absent, `1+` diminished, `2+` normal, `3+` brisk, `4+` with clonus. Brisk reflexes with an upgoing toe (a positive Babinski) mean an **upper motor neuron** problem, meaning brain or cord. Absent reflexes with flaccid, wasting muscle mean a **lower motor neuron** problem, meaning root or peripheral nerve.

### Complete, incomplete and the two shocks

A **complete** injury means no motor or sensory function below the level, including no sensation around the anus and no voluntary anal squeeze. An **incomplete** injury means some function is preserved, and the prognosis is far better. Checking sacral sparing is not optional, because it is often the only preserved function.

Two things called shock get confused constantly, and they are unrelated.

**Spinal shock** is a neurologic phenomenon: the cord below the injury temporarily stops working, giving flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes. It is not a blood pressure problem. It resolves over days to weeks, and the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex signals the end of it, after which the true extent of injury can be judged.

**Neurogenic shock** is a circulatory phenomenon. An injury above roughly `T6` cuts sympathetic outflow, so arterioles and veins dilate, SVR falls, and the heart cannot even mount a compensatory tachycardia because the cardiac accelerator fibers (`T1 to T4`) are cut too. The result is hypotension **with bradycardia** and warm, dry, pink skin below the lesion. It is the only shock state that looks like that. In a trauma patient, hemorrhage still has to be excluded first, and both can coexist.

### Cauda equina syndrome

Below `L1 to L2` there is no cord, only roots. Compress that bundle, most often with a large central disc herniation, and you get a surgical emergency: **saddle anesthesia** over the buttocks and inner thighs, **urinary retention with overflow incontinence**, bowel incontinence, bilateral leg weakness or sciatica, and loss of anal tone. Urinary retention is the most consistent finding. Delay costs permanent bladder and sexual function, so this is imaged urgently rather than treated conservatively.

> **Key:** Motor and dorsal column findings are ipsilateral in the cord; pain and temperature are contralateral. That is Brown-Sequard in one line.

> **Trap:** Spinal shock and neurogenic shock share a name and nothing else. One is absent reflexes, the other is hypotension with bradycardia.
keyPoints: Corticospinal and dorsal columns give ipsilateral findings in the cord; spinothalamic gives contralateral pain and temperature loss
Dermatome anchors: C4 shoulders, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 groin, L4 knee, S1 lateral foot
Reflex levels: biceps C5 to C6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1
Spinal shock is temporary flaccid areflexia; neurogenic shock is hypotension with bradycardia from lost sympathetic tone above T6
Cauda equina: saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, bilateral leg symptoms, lost anal tone, and it is a surgical emergency

checks.q: A stab wound to the right side of the cord at T6 produces which pattern?
choices: Bilateral weakness with preserved sensation
Right leg weakness and loss of vibration, with loss of pain and temperature in the left leg
Left leg weakness with right-sided loss of pain and temperature
Loss of all sensation below T6 with normal strength
checks.why: Brown-Sequard syndrome. The corticospinal tract and dorsal columns have not yet crossed in the cord, so weakness and vibration or position loss are ipsilateral. The spinothalamic tract crosses within a level or two of entry, so pain and temperature loss appear contralaterally.

checks.q: Which dermatome landmark is the umbilicus?
choices: T4
L1
S1
checks.why: T10 is the umbilicus. T4 is the nipple line, L1 the groin and S1 the lateral foot. These anchors let you assign a sensory level quickly in a trauma patient without a full dermatome chart.

checks.q: A 44-year-old has two days of severe low back pain, numbness across the buttocks and inner thighs, and has not urinated since yesterday. What is the concern?
choices: A simple lumbar strain, so treat with analgesia and follow up
Neurogenic shock
Cauda equina syndrome, requiring urgent imaging and surgical consultation
Spinal shock, which will resolve on its own
checks.why: Saddle anesthesia plus urinary retention is cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise, usually from a large central disc herniation compressing the nerve root bundle below L1. Retention is the most consistent finding, and delay causes permanent bladder and sexual dysfunction.

lessons.title: The autonomic nervous system, receptors and toxidromes
lessons.body:
## Two opposing wiring diagrams

The autonomic nervous system runs everything you do not think about, and it is the single most useful bridge between anatomy and pharmacology. Learn the receptors and half of emergency drug therapy explains itself.

**Sympathetic** fibers leave the cord from `T1` to `L2` (thoracolumbar), synapse in a chain of ganglia running alongside the spine, and then travel widely. Because the ganglia are close to the cord and the fibers diverge, sympathetic activation is a broadcast: the whole body responds at once. The adrenal medulla is a modified ganglion that dumps epinephrine straight into the blood, which is why the effect outlasts the nerve signal.

**Parasympathetic** fibers leave from the brainstem (cranial nerves III, VII, IX and especially X, the vagus) and from sacral roots `S2` to `S4` (craniosacral). Their ganglia sit on or in the target organ, so effects are targeted and local. The vagus alone supplies roughly `75%` of parasympathetic output, reaching heart, lungs and most of the gut.

Acetylcholine is the transmitter at every autonomic ganglion and at all parasympathetic endings. Norepinephrine is the transmitter at most sympathetic endings, with sweat glands as the odd exception.

### The receptors, and the drugs that hit them

| Receptor | Where | Effect when stimulated | Drugs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha-1 | Arteriolar and venous smooth muscle, pupil dilator | Vasoconstriction, raised SVR, mydriasis | Phenylephrine, norepinephrine; blocked by prazosin and tamsulosin |
| Alpha-2 | Presynaptic nerve terminals, brainstem | Reduces further norepinephrine release, lowers central sympathetic outflow | Clonidine, dexmedetomidine |
| Beta-1 | Heart, kidney juxtaglomerular cells | Raised heart rate, contractility and conduction; renin release | Dobutamine stimulates; metoprolol blocks |
| Beta-2 | Bronchial and vascular smooth muscle, uterus | Bronchodilation, vasodilation, tocolysis | Albuterol, terbutaline |
| Muscarinic | Heart, glands, smooth muscle | Slowed heart rate, secretions, bronchoconstriction, gut motility, pupil constriction | Blocked by atropine, glycopyrrolate; stimulated by pilocarpine |

Two memory hooks that hold up: one heart, two lungs (beta-1 is cardiac, beta-2 is pulmonary), and alpha squeezes.

Epinephrine deserves its own line because it hits all of them, and dose changes the balance. At the `0.3 mg` intramuscular dose for anaphylaxis it gives alpha-1 vasoconstriction to reverse the vasodilation and airway swelling, beta-1 support for the heart, and beta-2 bronchodilation, which is why one drug treats every part of that emergency at once.

### Toxidromes: patterns instead of guesswork

A toxidrome is the receptor picture reading backward from the patient. Five patterns cover most of what walks in.

**Sympathomimetic** (cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine). Tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils, agitation, and **sweaty** skin. Treat with benzodiazepines.

**Anticholinergic** (diphenhydramine, tricyclics, scopolamine, jimson weed). Nearly identical vitals, but the skin is **hot, dry and flushed** and the patient has urinary retention and absent bowel sounds. The classic string is mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, red as a beet, hot as a hare, dry as a bone. Sweating is the single sign that separates it from sympathomimetic.

**Cholinergic** (organophosphate pesticides, nerve agents, some mushrooms). Everything wet. **SLUDGE**: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal distress, emesis, plus bradycardia, bronchorrhea and miosis. Bronchial secretions, not the paralysis, are what kills. Atropine is the antidote and is titrated to drying the secretions, not to heart rate.

**Opioid** (heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone). The triad is **pinpoint pupils, depressed respirations and depressed consciousness**. Naloxone reverses it; the respiratory rate is the endpoint, not full wakefulness.

**Sedative-hypnotic** (benzodiazepines, alcohol, barbiturates). Depressed consciousness and slurred speech with relatively **normal pupils** and preserved vital signs until late.

> **Key:** Anticholinergic is dry and sympathomimetic is sweaty. The vitals look the same; the skin decides.

> **On the exam:** Pinpoint pupils appear in both opioid and cholinergic poisoning. The wet secretions and bradycardia of SLUDGE separate them.
keyPoints: Sympathetic is thoracolumbar T1 to L2 and broadcasts; parasympathetic is craniosacral and is targeted, mostly by the vagus
Alpha-1 constricts vessels, beta-1 drives the heart, beta-2 dilates bronchi, muscarinic slows and secretes
Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM works in anaphylaxis because it hits alpha-1, beta-1 and beta-2 at once
Anticholinergic is hot and dry; sympathomimetic is hot and sweaty; cholinergic SLUDGE is wet everywhere
Opioid toxidrome is pinpoint pupils with depressed respirations and consciousness, reversed by naloxone

checks.q: A patient sprayed a pesticide and now has copious drooling, tearing, vomiting, incontinence, wheezing and a heart rate of 44 with pinpoint pupils. Which toxidrome and which antidote endpoint?
choices: Sympathomimetic; give benzodiazepines until calm
Anticholinergic; give physostigmine until the skin sweats
Cholinergic; give atropine titrated to drying bronchial secretions
Opioid; give naloxone until the patient is fully awake
checks.why: SLUDGE with bradycardia and miosis is a cholinergic crisis from organophosphate poisoning. Bronchial secretions are the lethal feature, so atropine is titrated to drying them rather than to a heart rate target. Pralidoxime is added to regenerate the enzyme.

checks.q: Two agitated, tachycardic, hyperthermic patients with dilated pupils arrive. One is drenched in sweat and one is bone dry. What does that distinguish?
choices: The dry patient is anticholinergic and the sweaty patient is sympathomimetic
The dry patient is dehydrated and both are sympathomimetic
The sweaty patient is cholinergic
Nothing useful; both need the same treatment
checks.why: Sympathetic stimulation of sweat glands is cholinergic, so it survives in a sympathomimetic overdose and is blocked in an anticholinergic one. The vital signs and pupils look identical, so the skin is the discriminator, and it changes the antidote and the differential.

checks.q: Which receptor does albuterol primarily stimulate, and what is the effect?
choices: Alpha-1, causing vasoconstriction
Beta-1, raising heart rate and contractility
Muscarinic, increasing secretions
Beta-2, causing bronchodilation
checks.why: Beta-2 receptors relax bronchial smooth muscle, which is why albuterol opens airways. Its tremor and tachycardia come from beta-2 in skeletal muscle and vessels plus some beta-1 crossover at higher doses. Alpha-1 squeezes vessels and muscarinic stimulation would worsen bronchospasm.

lessons.title: The Glasgow Coma Scale and seizures
lessons.body:
## Scoring consciousness without arguing about words

The Glasgow Coma Scale exists because "lethargic" means different things to different people. It scores three behaviors and adds them, for a total of `3` to `15`. There is no zero in any category, so the minimum possible score is `3`.

**Eye opening, out of 4.** `4` spontaneous, `3` to voice, `2` to pressure, `1` none.

**Verbal response, out of 5.** `5` oriented, `4` confused conversation, `3` inappropriate words, `2` incomprehensible sounds, `1` none.

**Best motor response, out of 6.** `6` obeys commands, `5` localizes to pain, `4` normal flexion withdrawal, `3` abnormal flexion (decorticate), `2` extension (decerebrate), `1` none.

The motor score carries the most prognostic weight, which is why it is worth learning precisely. **Localizing** means the hand moves purposefully toward the stimulus, crossing the midline or reaching above the clavicle. **Withdrawal** pulls away without aiming. **Decorticate** flexes the arms in toward the core, meaning damage above the midbrain. **Decerebrate** extends and internally rotates the arms, meaning damage at or below the midbrain, and it is the worse of the two.

Rough bands: `13 to 15` is mild injury, `9 to 12` moderate, `8 or less` severe, with `8` the traditional threshold for considering a definitive airway.

The pitfalls matter as much as the scale. Score the **best** response, not the average or the worst side. An intubated patient cannot be scored verbally, so it is recorded as `T` for the verbal component rather than guessed at. Sedation, paralytics, alcohol, hypoglycemia and language barriers all corrupt the score, and a score without a recorded breakdown into its three parts is nearly useless, because a `9` made of `E2 V2 M5` is a very different patient from `E4 V1 M4`.

Children under about `2` cannot follow verbal instructions, so a **pediatric GCS** modifies the verbal scale to coos and babbles (`5`), irritable crying (`4`), crying to pain (`3`), moaning (`2`), none (`1`), and the eye and motor scales to age-appropriate behaviors.

### Seizures

A seizure is a burst of synchronized, uncontrolled electrical activity in the cortex, essentially excitation (glutamate) overwhelming inhibition (GABA). Classification starts with where it begins.

**Focal seizures** start in one area of one hemisphere. If awareness is preserved, the patient may describe twitching of one limb, an odd smell, deja vu or a rising sensation in the stomach. If awareness is impaired, the patient appears blank and may perform automatisms such as lip smacking or picking at clothing. A focal seizure can spread and become generalized.

**Generalized seizures** involve both hemispheres from the start. The **tonic-clonic** type is the recognizable one: a tonic phase of sustained stiffening for `10` to `20 seconds`, often with a cry as air is forced out and with apnea and cyanosis, then a clonic phase of rhythmic jerking for `30 seconds` to `2 minutes`, often with tongue biting on the side and incontinence, then a **postictal** period of confusion and sleepiness lasting minutes to hours. **Absence** seizures are brief blank stares of `5` to `15 seconds` with no postictal confusion, typically in school-age children and often mistaken for daydreaming.

**Status epilepticus** is defined operationally as `5 minutes` or more of continuous seizure activity, or two or more seizures without full recovery of consciousness between them. The five-minute definition replaced the older thirty-minute one because most seizures that will stop on their own do so within two minutes, and because damage begins early. The mechanism of that damage is excitotoxicity: continuous glutamate release floods neurons with calcium and kills them, while the systemic metabolic demand produces hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and hypoxia. After roughly `30 minutes`, GABA receptors also internalize, which is why benzodiazepines lose potency the longer a seizure runs. Treat early, at full dose.

Many seizures are **provoked** rather than epileptic, and those causes are correctable: hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypoxia, fever in young children, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, stimulant or tricyclic toxicity, head trauma, stroke, meningitis, and eclampsia in pregnancy or up to `6 weeks` postpartum.

> **Key:** Status epilepticus starts at `5 minutes`, not `30`. Every minute of delay makes benzodiazepines work less well.

> **On shift:** Check a glucose on every seizure patient before anything else. It is the fastest reversible cause on the list.
keyPoints: GCS is eye 4, verbal 5, motor 6, minimum score 3, and the motor component carries the most prognostic weight
Localizing crosses midline or reaches above the clavicle; decorticate flexes, decerebrate extends and is worse
Record the breakdown, score the best response, and mark verbal as T when intubated
Focal seizures start in one hemisphere and may or may not impair awareness; generalized involve both from the start
Status epilepticus is 5 minutes of seizure or repeat seizures without recovery, and GABA receptors internalize after about 30 minutes

checks.q: A patient opens eyes to pressure, makes incomprehensible sounds, and pulls his hand away from a painful stimulus without reaching for it. What is his GCS?
choices: GCS 8: E2 V2 M4
GCS 9: E2 V2 M5
GCS 7: E1 V2 M4
GCS 10: E3 V3 M4
checks.why: Eyes to pressure is 2, incomprehensible sounds is 2, and withdrawal without purposeful reaching is 4, totaling 8. Localizing (5) would require the hand to move toward the stimulus, crossing midline or reaching above the clavicle.

checks.q: Why is status epilepticus defined at 5 minutes rather than 30?
choices: Because scans cannot be obtained sooner
Because most self-limited seizures stop within about 2 minutes, and excitotoxic damage plus benzodiazepine resistance begin early
Because 5 minutes is the half-life of lorazepam
Because the postictal phase begins at 5 minutes
checks.why: Seizures that will terminate spontaneously almost always do so within roughly 2 minutes, so continued activity at 5 minutes predicts it will not stop on its own. Meanwhile glutamate-driven calcium influx is already killing neurons, and GABA receptors internalize over time, making benzodiazepines progressively less effective.

checks.q: Which posturing indicates the more caudal, more severe injury?
choices: Decorticate, arms flexed toward the core
Withdrawal from pain
Decerebrate, arms extended and internally rotated
Localizing to pain
checks.why: Decerebrate posturing (motor score 2) reflects damage at or below the midbrain and carries a worse prognosis than decorticate posturing (motor score 3), which reflects damage above it. Localizing and withdrawal are higher-scoring, less ominous responses.

lessons.title: Bone and muscle: structure, healing, fractures and the two emergencies
lessons.body:
## Bone is a living, negotiating organ

A long bone has a shaft (**diaphysis**), flared ends (**metaphysis**) and joint surfaces (**epiphysis**). In a growing child a cartilage **growth plate (physis)** sits between metaphysis and epiphysis. The outer shell is dense **cortical** bone; inside is spongy **cancellous** bone housing marrow. The **periosteum** carries the blood supply and the nerves, which is why fractures hurt and why stripped periosteum heals poorly.

Two cell types negotiate continuously: **osteoblasts** build and **osteoclasts** resorb. That remodeling never stops, which lets bone respond to load and explains why immobility and steroids weaken it.

Bone is also the body's **calcium bank**, holding about `99%` of total body calcium. When serum calcium falls, parathyroid hormone rises, osteoclasts release calcium, the kidney reabsorbs more and activates vitamin D, and the gut absorbs more. Calcitonin pushes the other way. That is why chronic kidney disease wrecks bone.

### Healing, and how long it really takes

1. **Hematoma**, hours to days. Bleeding from the broken ends clots into a scaffold.
2. **Soft callus**, day `1` to about `3 weeks`. Debris is cleared and cartilage bridges the gap. Still unstable.
3. **Hard callus**, about `3` to `12 weeks`. Cartilage becomes woven bone and the fracture unites clinically.
4. **Remodeling**, months to years, into organized lamellar bone along lines of stress.

Adult upper extremity fractures unite in about `6 weeks`, lower extremity in `12` or more, and children heal roughly twice as fast. Healing fails with poor blood supply, motion at the site, infection, wide separation, smoking, diabetes or malnutrition.

### Describing a fracture the way orthopedics does

A consult expects five things in order.

**Open or closed.** Open means the skin over the fracture is broken and the bone is contaminated, so: antibiotics early, tetanus, and urgent irrigation and debridement.

**Location.** Which bone, and proximal, middle or distal third.

**Pattern.** **Transverse** from a direct blow, **oblique** from angulation, **spiral** from twisting (in a non-ambulatory infant, a red flag for abuse), **comminuted** in three or more pieces from high energy, **segmental** with a free middle piece, and **greenstick** or **buckle** in children whose bone bends rather than snaps.

**Displacement, angulation, shortening, rotation.** Displacement is described by where the **distal** fragment sits, as a percentage of bone width. Angulation is named by where the apex points.

**Intra-articular or not.** A line entering the joint surface lowers the operative threshold, because a cartilage step-off leads to arthritis.

Children get their own system. **Salter-Harris** grades growth plate injuries `I` to `V`, as SALTR: `I` **S**traight across the physis, `II` **A**bove into the metaphysis (by far the most common), `III` be**L**ow into the epiphysis and joint, `IV` **T**hrough both, `V` c**R**ush. Higher numbers risk growth arrest, and type `V` is the worst and the hardest to see because alignment can look normal. A growth plate injury can leave a limb permanently short or angled, so tenderness over a physis is treated as a fracture even with normal films.

Two fractures need little force. A **pathologic** fracture goes through bone weakened by tumor, infection, osteoporosis or cyst, sometimes with no trauma. A **stress** fracture is microdamage from repetitive loading outpacing remodeling, classically tibia or metatarsals in a new runner, often invisible on early films.

### Muscle, and the two ways it turns dangerous

Muscle contracts when an action potential releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, calcium clears the regulatory proteins off actin, and myosin heads pull the filaments past each other using ATP. No ATP means the heads cannot release, which is rigor mortis.

**Rhabdomyolysis** is muscle breakdown releasing creatine kinase, myoglobin, potassium and phosphate into blood, after crush injury, prolonged immobilization, extreme exertion, seizures, hyperthermia or statins. `CK` above roughly `5 times` normal makes the diagnosis. Myoglobin injures kidneys, so aggressive IV fluid is the treatment, and the released potassium can be lethal.

**Compartment syndrome** is pressure rising inside a closed fascial space until it exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, so muscle and nerve die while the pulse is still present. Of the five Ps, pallor, pulselessness and paralysis are late and useless for diagnosis. The two that come first are **pain out of proportion** and **pain with passive stretch** of that compartment's muscles. Normal pressure is under `10 mmHg`; fasciotomy is generally indicated above about `30 mmHg`, or when diastolic minus compartment pressure is under `30`. Irreversible damage begins within `4` to `6 hours`.

> **Key:** Waiting for pulselessness in compartment syndrome means waiting until the limb is already lost. Pain with passive stretch is the early sign.

> **Trap:** A normal x-ray does not exclude a growth plate injury or a stress fracture. Both are diagnosed by where it hurts.
keyPoints: Osteoblasts build and osteoclasts resorb; bone holds about 99% of body calcium under PTH control
Healing: hematoma, soft callus to about 3 weeks, hard callus 3 to 12 weeks, then remodeling for months
Describe fractures as open or closed, location, pattern, displacement and angulation, and intra-articular or not
Salter-Harris SALTR I to V; higher numbers risk growth arrest and type V is easiest to miss
Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch come first; fasciotomy above about 30 mmHg

checks.q: Six hours after a tibial shaft fracture was splinted, a patient needs escalating opioid doses and screams when the toes are passively extended. Pulses are present. What is happening?
choices: Normal fracture pain; increase analgesia and reassess in the morning
Compartment syndrome; pulses stay present until very late
Deep vein thrombosis
Fat embolism syndrome
checks.why: Compartment pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure long before it exceeds arterial pressure, so pulses persist while muscle dies. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the early findings, and irreversible damage begins within 4 to 6 hours.

checks.q: A 9-year-old has a fracture line running across the growth plate and extending up into the metaphysis. Which Salter-Harris type?
choices: Type I
Type III
Type II
Type V
checks.why: SALTR: type II is Above, through the physis and out into the metaphysis, and it is the most common. Type I is straight across the physis alone, type III extends below into the epiphysis and joint, and type V is a crush injury with often normal-looking alignment.

checks.q: A patient found down on a hard floor for 14 hours has tea-colored urine and a CK of 42,000. What is the priority?
choices: Aggressive IV fluid to protect the kidneys, with attention to potassium
Immediate fasciotomy of all four leg compartments
Oral hydration and discharge with follow-up
Diuretics to flush the myoglobin
checks.why: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin that injures renal tubules and potassium that can cause arrest. Aggressive isotonic fluid is the mainstay, and potassium must be monitored. Fasciotomy is for confirmed compartment syndrome, and diuretics before volume repletion make renal injury worse.

lessons.title: Joint by joint, the back, and the exam that sorts them
lessons.body:
## Three tissues that get confused

A **ligament** connects bone to bone for stability, and tearing one is a **sprain**. A **tendon** connects muscle to bone, and tearing one is a **strain**. Both have poor blood supply, so they heal slowly compared with bone. Cartilage has no blood supply at all, so it essentially does not repair.

### The injuries, by joint

| Injury | Mechanism | Exam finding that names it |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior shoulder dislocation | Abduction with external rotation | Squared-off shoulder, arm slightly abducted, resists internal rotation; check axillary nerve sensation |
| AC separation | Fall onto the point of the shoulder | Step-off at the AC joint, pain on cross-body adduction |
| Rotator cuff tear | Overhead use, or a fall on the arm | Weak abduction and external rotation, positive drop arm, night pain |
| Elbow dislocation | Fall on an outstretched hand | Deformity, lost olecranon triangle; check brachial artery and ulnar nerve |
| Nursemaid's elbow | Pull on a toddler's extended, pronated arm | Arm held flexed and pronated, unused, with no swelling |
| Distal radius (Colles') | Fall on an outstretched hand | Dinner-fork deformity; check median nerve |
| Scaphoid fracture | Fall on an outstretched hand | Snuffbox tenderness, often normal x-ray, so splint and re-image |
| Boxer's fracture | Punching with a closed fist | Depressed fifth knuckle; look for a tooth wound |
| Hip fracture | Fall in an older adult | Leg shortened and externally rotated, cannot bear weight |
| ACL tear | Pivot or deceleration on a planted foot | Pop, rapid hemarthrosis, positive Lachman |
| PCL tear | Dashboard blow driving the tibia back | Posterior sag, positive posterior drawer |
| MCL tear | Blow to the outside of the knee | Medial joint line pain, laxity on valgus stress |
| Meniscus tear | Twisting a loaded, flexed knee | Joint line tenderness, locking, slow effusion, positive McMurray |
| Patellar dislocation | Twisting on a planted foot | Patella displaced laterally, knee held flexed, later apprehension sign |
| Ankle sprain | Inversion of a plantarflexed foot | Anterior talofibular tenderness; grades I stretch, II partial, III complete |
| Achilles rupture | Sudden push-off, middle-aged athlete | Palpable gap, positive Thompson: calf squeeze fails to plantarflex |
| Lisfranc injury | Axial load on a plantarflexed foot | Midfoot swelling, plantar bruising, widening at the first and second metatarsal bases |

The **Ottawa ankle rules** exist because most sprained ankles do not need imaging. X-ray the ankle only for bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps both immediately and in the department. X-ray the foot only for tenderness at the fifth metatarsal base or the navicular, or that same weight-bearing failure. Applied properly they are close to `100%` sensitive for significant fractures.

### The back

Between vertebrae sit discs: a tough outer ring (**annulus fibrosus**) around a gel center (**nucleus pulposus**). With age or load the ring weakens and the gel pushes out backward and to one side, where the nerve root sits. About `95%` of these **herniated discs** are at `L4 to L5` or `L5 to S1`.

The result is **radiculopathy**: pain down the leg past the knee in that root's distribution, with numbness or weakness, worse sitting, coughing or straining. A straight leg raise reproducing leg pain at `30` to `70 degrees` supports it. `L5` weakens big toe and ankle dorsiflexion; `S1` weakens plantar flexion and drops the Achilles reflex.

Most back pain is mechanical and improves. The job is finding the fraction that is not, using **red flags**: age over `50` or under `18`, fever, unexplained weight loss, cancer history, IV drug use, significant trauma, immunosuppression, night pain unrelieved by rest, progressive deficit, and above all saddle anesthesia with urinary retention, which is **cauda equina syndrome**.

### The musculoskeletal exam sequence

Same order every time. **Inspection** for deformity, swelling, bruising and skin breaks, comparing sides. **Palpation** for point tenderness, crepitus and effusion, working toward the painful spot rather than starting on it. **Range of motion**, active first because it is safer, then passive. **Strength** `0` none, `1` flicker, `2` with gravity eliminated, `3` against gravity, `4` against some resistance, `5` normal. **Neurovascular check** distal to the injury, documented before and after any splint. Then **special tests** last, because they are provocative.

> **Key:** A hemarthrosis within hours means bleeding inside the joint, most often an ACL tear. A slow effusion over a day suggests a meniscus.

> **On shift:** Document distal pulses, sensation and motor before and after every splint. If it was not documented before, you cannot prove the splint did not cause it.
keyPoints: Sprain is a ligament, strain is a tendon, and cartilage has no blood supply so it does not repair
ACL: pop, rapid hemarthrosis, positive Lachman; meniscus: locking, joint line tenderness, slow effusion
Snuffbox tenderness means scaphoid fracture despite a normal x-ray; splint and re-image
Ottawa ankle rules: image only for malleolar, fifth metatarsal base or navicular tenderness, or inability to take four steps
Exam order: inspection, palpation, active then passive range of motion, strength 0 to 5, neurovascular check, special tests

checks.q: A 24-year-old pivoted while playing soccer, heard a pop, and the knee swelled within two hours. Which injury and which test?
choices: Meniscus tear; McMurray test
ACL tear; Lachman test
MCL tear; valgus stress test
Patellar dislocation; apprehension sign
checks.why: A non-contact pivoting injury with an audible pop and a rapid effusion is a hemarthrosis from an ACL tear, and Lachman is the most sensitive test for it. Meniscal effusions build slowly over a day, MCL injury follows a blow to the outside of the knee, and patellar dislocation is usually visibly deformed.

checks.q: A patient fell on an outstretched hand and is tender in the anatomic snuffbox, but the x-ray is read as normal. What should happen?
choices: Discharge with reassurance since the film is negative
Immediate surgical fixation
Splint as a presumed scaphoid fracture and arrange repeat imaging
Treat as a wrist sprain with early range of motion
checks.why: Scaphoid fractures are frequently invisible on initial films, and the scaphoid's blood supply enters distally, so a missed fracture risks avascular necrosis and nonunion. Snuffbox tenderness is treated as a fracture until repeat imaging or advanced imaging says otherwise.

checks.q: Which finding in low back pain most urgently demands imaging and a surgical consult?
choices: Pain radiating below the knee with a positive straight leg raise
Saddle anesthesia with new urinary retention
Pain that worsens with sitting and coughing
Paraspinal muscle spasm and limited flexion
checks.why: Saddle anesthesia with urinary retention is cauda equina syndrome, where a large central disc compresses the nerve root bundle, and delay causes permanent bladder and sexual dysfunction. Radicular leg pain with a positive straight leg raise is a common herniated disc, usually managed without emergency surgery.

cards.front: What is the resting membrane potential of a neuron and what maintains it?
cards.back: About -70 mV inside relative to outside, held by the sodium-potassium ATPase pumping three sodium out for every two potassium in. It costs ATP continuously, which is why neurons die fast without perfusion.

cards.front: Walk through the voltages of an action potential.
cards.back: Rest about -70 mV, threshold about -55 mV, sodium rushes in and the inside swings to about +30 mV, then potassium leaves and the cell repolarizes with a brief hyperpolarizing overshoot.

cards.front: How does myelin speed conduction, and what makes the myelin in the brain versus the peripheral nerves?
cards.back: Impulses jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), reaching up to 120 m/s versus 0.5 to 2 m/s unmyelinated. Oligodendrocytes myelinate centrally, Schwann cells peripherally.

cards.front: Which diseases strip myelin centrally and peripherally?
cards.back: Multiple sclerosis attacks central myelin; Guillain-Barre syndrome attacks peripheral myelin, ascending from the feet and threatening the diaphragm.

cards.front: Which transmitter is the brain's main brake and which is the main accelerator?
cards.back: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter, enhanced by benzodiazepines. Glutamate is the main excitatory one, blocked at NMDA receptors by ketamine. A seizure is that balance tipping toward glutamate.

cards.front: Name a drug that targets acetylcholine, dopamine and serotonin respectively.
cards.back: Atropine blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Levodopa replaces dopamine and haloperidol blocks it. SSRIs such as sertraline block serotonin reuptake.

cards.front: What deficits follow a frontal lobe injury?
cards.back: Contralateral weakness from the motor strip, expressive (Broca's) aphasia if the dominant side, and changes in judgment, planning, personality and impulse control that families notice first.

cards.front: Contrast Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia.
cards.back: Broca's is dominant frontal: effortful, sparse speech with preserved comprehension and obvious frustration. Wernicke's is dominant temporal: fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension and little insight.

cards.front: What is neglect and which hemisphere produces it?
cards.back: Failure to acknowledge one side of the world, including the patient's own limb, from a non-dominant (usually right) parietal lesion. Language lives on the left in about 95% of right-handed people.

cards.front: What causes Parkinson's disease and what are its four cardinal features?
cards.back: Loss of dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra, disrupting basal ganglia output. Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability. Levodopa replaces dopamine; antipsychotics can mimic it.

cards.front: What does the reticular activating system do, and what does the cortex add?
cards.back: The RAS runs through the brainstem into the thalamus and generates arousal, being awake at all. The cortex supplies content, making sense. A patient can have one without the other.

cards.front: How do structural and metabolic causes of altered mental status differ on exam?
cards.back: Structural causes (bleed, mass, stroke) press on one area, producing focal findings and unequal pupils. Metabolic or toxic causes hit the whole brain, producing symmetric findings with equal reactive pupils.

cards.front: Separate delirium, dementia and psychosis.
cards.back: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, attention-impaired and medically caused. Dementia is chronic and progressive with memory loss and preserved attention until late. Psychosis distorts content with intact orientation and rarely begins after age 40.

cards.front: Name the three meningeal layers from outside in.
cards.back: Dura mater, the tough layer against the skull; arachnoid mater beneath it; pia mater glued to the brain surface. CSF sits in the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia.

cards.front: Describe an epidural hematoma: vessel, course and CT appearance.
cards.back: Arterial, usually the middle meningeal artery from a temporal bone fracture. Brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid decline. Convex lens shape that does not cross suture lines.

cards.front: Describe a subdural hematoma: vessel, population and CT appearance.
cards.back: Torn bridging veins, so slow. Typical in the elderly and heavy drinkers whose brain atrophy stretches those veins, presenting over days to weeks. Crescent shaped, and it does cross suture lines.

cards.front: How does a subarachnoid hemorrhage present and how is it worked up?
cards.back: Thunderclap worst-ever headache at maximal intensity within seconds, often with neck stiffness, vomiting and photophobia. CT within 6 hours is highly sensitive; after that, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia.

cards.front: State the Monro-Kellie doctrine and its three contents.
cards.back: The skull is a fixed box holding brain (about 80%), blood (about 10%) and CSF (about 10%). Add anything and one must be displaced or pressure rises. CSF is pushed out first, then venous blood, then compensation ends abruptly.

cards.front: Give normal ICP, the treatment threshold, and the formula for cerebral perfusion pressure.
cards.back: Normal ICP 5 to 15 mmHg, treat generally above 20 to 22. CPP = MAP - ICP, target above about 60 mmHg. Hypotension damages the brain as surely as high ICP does.

cards.front: What is Cushing's triad and what does it mean?
cards.back: Rising systolic pressure with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular breathing. The body raising MAP to preserve CPP, with a baroreflex answer. It is a late sign of brainstem compression.

cards.front: What happens in uncal herniation, and why is hyperventilation only a bridge?
cards.back: The medial temporal lobe presses on cranial nerve III, giving a fixed dilated pupil on the same side as the lesion with contralateral weakness. Hyperventilation to EtCO2 30 to 35 lowers ICP by constricting vessels, but also cuts cerebral blood flow.

cards.front: Which vessels make up the anterior and posterior cerebral circulations?
cards.back: Anterior: the two internal carotids, each dividing into MCA and ACA. Posterior: the two vertebrals joining as the basilar, which supplies brainstem and cerebellum and splits into the two PCAs.

cards.front: What is the Circle of Willis for, and why is it clinically inconsistent?
cards.back: A collateral ring joining anterior and posterior circulations through the anterior and posterior communicating arteries. It is complete in only about 20 to 50% of people, so identical occlusions cause different deficits.

cards.front: Describe the classic MCA stroke syndrome.
cards.back: Contralateral face and arm weakness and numbness worse than the leg, aphasia if the dominant hemisphere, neglect if non-dominant, and gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion.

cards.front: How do ACA and PCA strokes differ from MCA strokes?
cards.back: ACA supplies the medial leg area, so the leg is weaker than the arm, sometimes with incontinence and abulia. PCA supplies the occipital lobe and thalamus, giving a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with often normal strength.

cards.front: What are the warning features of a posterior circulation stroke?
cards.back: The Ds: dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria and dysphagia, plus ataxia, crossed findings and inability to sit unsupported. Dizziness that travels in company is a brainstem problem, not an inner ear one.

cards.front: What is the ischemic penumbra?
cards.back: Tissue around the dead core that has lost enough flow to stop working but not enough to die yet, kept alive by collaterals. It is silent but salvageable, and it is the entire target of stroke treatment.

cards.front: Why is 'last known well' the critical time, and what are the treatment windows?
cards.back: It is the last moment the patient was at baseline, and windows run from it: thrombolysis generally within 4.5 hours, thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours in selected patients with salvageable penumbra.

cards.front: How do you distinguish Bell's palsy from a stroke on facial exam?
cards.back: Ask the patient to raise both eyebrows. The forehead has bilateral cortical input, so a stroke spares it. A peripheral facial nerve palsy takes the whole half of the face including forehead and eye closure.

cards.front: Which cranial nerves control eye movement and what does each do?
cards.back: CN III most movements plus eyelid and pupil constriction, CN IV superior oblique (down and in), CN VI lateral rectus (abduction). The mnemonic is LR6 SO4, all the rest 3.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve fails early with raised intracranial pressure, and how does it show?
cards.back: CN VI, the abducens, because it has the longest intracranial course. The eye cannot abduct and the patient sees horizontal double vision. It is a false localizing sign.

cards.front: Which nerve carries light into the pupil reflex and which carries constriction out?
cards.back: CN II (optic) is the afferent limb and CN III (oculomotor) is the efferent limb. A pupil that constricts consensually but not directly has an optic problem; a fixed dilated pupil in an eye that sees is a CN III problem.

cards.front: Give the neurological exam sequence in order.
cards.back: Mental status, cranial nerves, motor, sensory, reflexes, coordination, gait. Gait is the most informative single test because it needs motor, sensory, cerebellar and vestibular systems working together.

cards.front: What does 'focal deficit' mean and what does it imply?
cards.back: A finding that maps to one specific location, such as one limb, one visual field or one cranial nerve. Focal favors a structural cause like stroke, bleed or mass; global symmetric findings favor metabolic or toxic causes.

cards.front: Name the three main spinal cord tracts and which side each serves.
cards.back: Corticospinal carries motor down and crosses in the medulla, so cord lesions weaken the same side. Dorsal columns carry vibration and position up uncrossed, same side. Spinothalamic carries pain and temperature and crosses at entry, opposite side.

cards.front: What does a hemisection of the cord (Brown-Sequard) produce?
cards.back: Ipsilateral weakness, ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning a level or two below the lesion.

cards.front: Give the six dermatome anchors.
cards.back: C4 top of the shoulders, T4 nipple line, T10 umbilicus, L1 groin, L4 kneecap and medial shin, S1 lateral foot and little toe.

cards.front: Give the levels for the biceps, triceps, patellar and Achilles reflexes.
cards.back: Biceps C5 to C6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1. Graded 0 absent, 1+ diminished, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ with clonus.

cards.front: How do upper and lower motor neuron findings differ?
cards.back: Upper motor neuron (brain or cord): brisk reflexes, increased tone, upgoing toe on Babinski. Lower motor neuron (root or peripheral nerve): absent reflexes, flaccid tone, atrophy and fasciculations.
