cards.front: What distinguishes a complete from an incomplete cord injury, and why check sacral function?
cards.back: Complete means no motor or sensory function below the level, including no perianal sensation and no voluntary anal squeeze. Sacral sparing is often the only preserved function and changes the prognosis substantially.

cards.front: Contrast spinal shock with neurogenic shock.
cards.back: Spinal shock is neurologic: temporary flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes below the injury, resolving over days to weeks. Neurogenic shock is circulatory: hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin from lost sympathetic outflow above about T6.

cards.front: What are the features of cauda equina syndrome?
cards.back: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention with overflow incontinence, bowel incontinence, bilateral leg weakness or sciatica, and lost anal tone. Retention is the most consistent finding, and it is a surgical emergency.

cards.front: Where do sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers leave the central nervous system?
cards.back: Sympathetic from T1 to L2 (thoracolumbar) into a paravertebral ganglion chain, so effects broadcast widely. Parasympathetic from cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X plus S2 to S4 (craniosacral), with ganglia on the organ, so effects are local.

cards.front: What does alpha-1 stimulation do and which drugs hit it?
cards.back: Constricts arterioles and veins and dilates the pupil, raising SVR and blood pressure. Phenylephrine and norepinephrine stimulate it; prazosin and tamsulosin block it.

cards.front: Contrast beta-1 and beta-2 effects and name a drug for each.
cards.back: One heart, two lungs. Beta-1 raises heart rate, contractility and conduction and releases renin (dobutamine stimulates, metoprolol blocks). Beta-2 dilates bronchi and vessels and relaxes the uterus (albuterol, terbutaline).

cards.front: What do muscarinic receptors do and which drugs block them?
cards.back: Slow the heart, increase secretions, constrict bronchi, increase gut motility and constrict pupils. Atropine and glycopyrrolate block them; pilocarpine stimulates them.

cards.front: Why does one drug treat every part of anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM hits alpha-1 to reverse vasodilation and reduce airway swelling, beta-1 to support the heart, and beta-2 to bronchodilate, all at once.

cards.front: What single sign separates the anticholinergic from the sympathomimetic toxidrome?
cards.back: Sweating. Both give tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils and agitation, but sympathomimetic skin is drenched while anticholinergic skin is hot, dry and flushed, with retention and absent bowel sounds.

cards.front: What does SLUDGE stand for and what actually kills in cholinergic poisoning?
cards.back: Salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal distress, emesis, plus bradycardia and miosis. Bronchial secretions kill, so atropine is titrated to drying secretions rather than to heart rate.

cards.front: Give the opioid and sedative-hypnotic toxidromes.
cards.back: Opioid: pinpoint pupils, depressed respirations and depressed consciousness, reversed by naloxone with respiratory rate as the endpoint. Sedative-hypnotic: depressed consciousness and slurred speech with normal pupils and preserved vitals until late.

cards.front: Give the three components of the Glasgow Coma Scale and their maximums.
cards.back: Eye opening out of 4, verbal response out of 5, best motor response out of 6, for a total of 3 to 15. There is no zero in any category, so 3 is the minimum.

cards.front: List the six GCS motor responses.
cards.back: 6 obeys commands, 5 localizes to pain, 4 normal flexion withdrawal, 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate), 2 extension (decerebrate), 1 none. The motor score carries the most prognostic weight.

cards.front: How do you tell localizing from withdrawal, and decorticate from decerebrate?
cards.back: Localizing moves purposefully toward the stimulus, crossing midline or reaching above the clavicle; withdrawal just pulls away. Decorticate flexes arms toward the core (above midbrain); decerebrate extends and internally rotates (at or below midbrain, worse).

cards.front: What are the main GCS scoring pitfalls?
cards.back: Score the best response, not the worst side or an average. Record the three components separately, since 9 as E2 V2 M5 differs from E4 V1 M4. Mark verbal as T when intubated. Sedation, alcohol and hypoglycemia all corrupt it.

cards.front: How are seizures classified, and what happens in a tonic-clonic?
cards.back: Focal (one hemisphere, awareness preserved or impaired) versus generalized (both from the start). Tonic-clonic: 10 to 20 s of stiffening with apnea, then 30 s to 2 min of jerking, then minutes to hours of postictal confusion.

cards.front: Define status epilepticus and explain why the definition changed to 5 minutes.
cards.back: Five minutes or more of continuous seizure, or repeat seizures without recovery between. Most self-limited seizures stop within 2 minutes, excitotoxic calcium injury starts early, and GABA receptors internalize by about 30 minutes so benzodiazepines weaken.

cards.front: Name the common provoked, correctable causes of seizure.
cards.back: Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypoxia, fever in young children, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, stimulant or tricyclic toxicity, head trauma, stroke, meningitis, and eclampsia up to 6 weeks postpartum.

cards.front: Name the four phases of fracture healing with their timelines.
cards.back: Hematoma over hours to days, inflammation and soft callus from day 1 to about 3 weeks, hard callus about 3 to 12 weeks, then remodeling over months to years. Upper limb unites around 6 weeks, lower limb 12 or more.

cards.front: How does bone act as a calcium bank?
cards.back: It holds about 99% of body calcium. Low serum calcium raises parathyroid hormone, which activates osteoclasts, increases renal reabsorption and activates vitamin D for gut absorption. Calcitonin opposes it.

cards.front: What five things does an orthopedic fracture description include?
cards.back: Open or closed, location by bone and third, pattern, displacement and angulation and shortening or rotation, and whether the line enters the joint. Displacement is described by where the distal fragment sits.

cards.front: Name the fracture patterns and the force behind each.
cards.back: Transverse from a direct blow, oblique from angulation, spiral from twisting, comminuted (three or more pieces) from high energy, segmental with a free middle piece, and greenstick or buckle in children.

cards.front: Give the Salter-Harris classification and why it matters.
cards.back: SALTR: I Straight across the physis, II Above into metaphysis (most common), III beLow into epiphysis and joint, IV Through both, V cRush. Higher numbers risk growth arrest; V is the worst and the easiest to miss.

cards.front: Distinguish a pathologic from a stress fracture.
cards.back: Pathologic occurs through bone already weakened by tumor, infection, osteoporosis or cyst, sometimes without trauma. Stress is accumulated microdamage from repetitive load, classically tibia or metatarsals in a new runner, often invisible on early films.

cards.front: What is rhabdomyolysis, what confirms it, and what is the treatment?
cards.back: Muscle breakdown releasing CK, myoglobin, potassium and phosphate after crush, immobilization, extreme exertion, seizures or statins. CK above roughly 5 times normal confirms it. Aggressive IV fluid protects the kidney; watch potassium.

cards.front: What are the early signs of compartment syndrome and the pressure numbers?
cards.back: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch come first; pallor, pulselessness and paralysis are late. Normal pressure is under 10 mmHg, fasciotomy generally above 30, or delta pressure under 30. Damage begins in 4 to 6 hours.

cards.front: Distinguish sprain, strain and cartilage injury.
cards.back: A sprain tears a ligament (bone to bone), a strain tears a tendon or muscle (muscle to bone). Both heal slowly because of poor blood supply. Cartilage has no blood supply at all, so it essentially does not repair.

cards.front: How do ACL and meniscus injuries differ in mechanism and effusion?
cards.back: ACL: pivoting or decelerating on a planted foot, audible pop, rapid hemarthrosis within hours, positive Lachman. Meniscus: twisting on a loaded flexed knee, joint line tenderness, locking or catching, slow effusion over a day, positive McMurray.

cards.front: Why is snuffbox tenderness treated as a fracture even with a normal x-ray?
cards.back: Scaphoid fractures are often invisible on initial films, and the scaphoid's blood supply enters distally, so a missed fracture risks avascular necrosis and nonunion. Splint and repeat imaging.

cards.front: State the Ottawa ankle rules.
cards.back: X-ray the ankle for bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps both immediately and in the department. X-ray the foot for tenderness at the fifth metatarsal base or navicular, or the same weight-bearing failure.

cards.front: What is the Thompson test and what does it detect?
cards.back: Squeeze the calf with the patient prone and the foot hanging. Normally the foot plantarflexes. No movement means a ruptured Achilles tendon, often with a palpable gap, classically after a sudden push-off.

cards.front: Which findings suggest an anterior shoulder dislocation and what nerve must be checked?
cards.back: Squared-off shoulder with loss of the deltoid contour, arm held slightly abducted and externally rotated, resisting internal rotation. Check axillary nerve sensation over the lateral deltoid before and after reduction.

cards.front: Where do most disc herniations occur, and what does each root deficit look like?
cards.back: About 95% at L4 to L5 or L5 to S1. L5 weakens big toe and ankle dorsiflexion; S1 weakens plantar flexion and reduces the Achilles reflex. Straight leg raise reproducing leg pain at 30 to 70 degrees supports radiculopathy.

cards.front: List the back pain red flags.
cards.back: Age over 50 or under 18 with new pain, fever, unexplained weight loss, cancer history, IV drug use, significant trauma, immunosuppression, night pain unrelieved by rest, progressive deficit, and saddle anesthesia with retention.

cards.front: Give the musculoskeletal exam sequence and the strength grading scale.
cards.back: Inspection, palpation, active then passive range of motion, strength, neurovascular check, special tests last. Strength: 0 none, 1 flicker, 2 movement with gravity eliminated, 3 against gravity, 4 against some resistance, 5 normal.

quiz.q: Which statement about the action potential is correct?
choices: It is all-or-none, and signal strength is coded by firing frequency
A stronger stimulus produces a larger spike
It travels equally fast in myelinated and unmyelinated fibers
It occurs without any energy cost to the neuron
quiz.why: Reaching threshold near -55 mV produces a full-size spike every time, so intensity is encoded by how often and how many neurons fire. Myelin increases speed dramatically, and maintaining the gradient costs continuous ATP through the sodium-potassium pump.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has progressive weakness beginning in both feet and ascending over three days, with absent reflexes, two weeks after a diarrheal illness. What is the underlying problem and the main danger?
choices: Dopamine depletion; risk of falls
Upper motor neuron cord compression; risk of paralysis
Peripheral demyelination; risk of diaphragm involvement and respiratory failure
Neuromuscular junction antibody blockade; risk of ptosis
quiz.why: This is Guillain-Barre syndrome. Loss of peripheral myelin removes saltatory conduction, producing symmetric ascending weakness with absent reflexes. The danger is ascent to the phrenic nerve and diaphragm, so serial vital capacity is monitored rather than relying on saturation.

quiz.q: Lorazepam stops a seizure by acting on which transmitter system?
choices: Blocking glutamate at NMDA receptors
Enhancing GABA, the brain's main inhibitory transmitter
Replacing dopamine in the basal ganglia
Blocking acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors
quiz.why: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA, restoring the brake against runaway glutamate excitation. Ketamine blocks NMDA glutamate receptors, levodopa replaces dopamine, and atropine blocks muscarinic receptors.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old speaks in fluent but meaningless sentences and does not seem to notice anything is wrong. Comprehension is poor. Where is the lesion?
choices: Non-dominant parietal lobe
Dominant frontal lobe
Cerebellum
Dominant temporal lobe
quiz.why: Wernicke's area in the dominant temporal lobe handles comprehension, so damage leaves speech fluent but empty with little insight. A dominant frontal (Broca's) lesion produces effortful, sparse speech with preserved understanding and visible frustration.

quiz.q: A patient has a left-sided intention tremor, left-sided dysmetria on finger-to-nose, and a wide-based gait. Where is the lesion and on which side?
choices: Right motor cortex
Left cerebellar hemisphere
Right basal ganglia
Left parietal lobe
quiz.why: Cerebellar hemispheres control the same side of the body, so left-sided ataxia and dysmetria mean a left cerebellar lesion. Cortical motor and sensory findings cross, and basal ganglia disease gives resting tremor with rigidity rather than intention tremor.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident is newly confused, worse in the evenings, cannot sustain attention, and has equal reactive pupils with no focal weakness. What is the most appropriate framing?
choices: Progressive dementia requiring outpatient follow-up
New-onset psychosis requiring psychiatric admission
Delirium from a medical cause that must be identified
A structural lesion until imaging proves otherwise
quiz.why: Acute onset with fluctuation and impaired attention defines delirium. Symmetric findings with reactive pupils point to a global metabolic or toxic cause such as infection, glucose, sodium or a medication. Dementia is chronic and progressive, and first-episode psychosis after 40 is rare.

quiz.q: Which vessel is classically torn in an epidural hematoma?
choices: Middle meningeal artery
Bridging veins
Anterior communicating artery
Basilar artery
quiz.why: The middle meningeal artery runs beneath the thin temporal bone and tears with temporal fractures, filling the epidural space at arterial pressure. Bridging veins produce subdural bleeding, and berry aneurysms of the communicating arteries produce subarachnoid hemorrhage.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient has an ICP of 25 mmHg and a MAP of 75 mmHg. What is the CPP and what does it require?
choices: 100 mmHg; no intervention
25 mmHg; treat the ICP only
75 mmHg; the ICP can be ignored
50 mmHg; below target, so lower ICP and support MAP
quiz.why: CPP = MAP - ICP = 75 - 25 = 50 mmHg, below the usual target above 60. The equation has two terms, so allowing hypotension is as harmful as allowing intracranial hypertension. Both must be managed.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old on warfarin has three weeks of worsening headache and confusion after a fall she barely remembers. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines. Which bleed, and why this presentation?
choices: Epidural, because arterial bleeding is rapid
Subarachnoid, because aneurysms rupture suddenly
Subdural, because low-pressure bridging vein bleeding accumulates slowly in an atrophic brain
Intraventricular, because CSF flow is obstructed
quiz.why: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins, so minor trauma tears them, and venous pressure fills the subdural space slowly over days to weeks. The crescent shape crossing sutures is diagnostic, since the collection lies inside the dura. Epidural bleeds are convex and do not cross sutures.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient's blood pressure rises from 130/80 to 190/70 while the heart rate falls from 88 to 46 and breathing becomes irregular. What does this indicate?
choices: Adequate resuscitation and improving perfusion
Cushing's triad from critically raised intracranial pressure
Neurogenic shock from an associated cord injury
A vasovagal response to pain
quiz.why: Cushing's triad is rising systolic pressure with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations. It is the body raising MAP to preserve CPP, with a baroreflex bradycardia in answer. It is a late sign of brainstem compression, not a reassuring one.

quiz.q: A patient has left facial droop, left arm weakness, a nearly normal left leg, and does not acknowledge the left side of the room. Which vessel and hemisphere?
choices: Right middle cerebral artery
Left middle cerebral artery
Right anterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery
quiz.why: Face and arm weakness out of proportion to the leg is MCA territory, and deficits are contralateral, so a left-sided deficit means a right-sided lesion. Neglect confirms the non-dominant hemisphere. ACA strokes hit the leg, and PCA strokes take visual fields.

quiz.q: Which artery system supplies the brainstem and cerebellum?
choices: Internal carotid to middle cerebral artery
Internal carotid to anterior cerebral artery
Anterior communicating artery
Vertebral arteries joining to form the basilar artery
quiz.why: The two vertebral arteries merge into the basilar, which supplies the brainstem and cerebellum before splitting into the posterior cerebral arteries. The carotids supply the anterior circulation, and the communicating arteries are collateral connections, not territory suppliers.

quiz.q: A patient has marked right leg weakness, a normal right arm and face, urinary incontinence and apathy. Which vessel is occluded?
choices: Right middle cerebral artery
Left middle cerebral artery
Left anterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery
quiz.why: The homunculus places the leg on the medial surface, which is ACA territory, so leg weakness out of proportion to the arm plus incontinence and abulia is an ACA stroke. Deficits cross, so a right-sided deficit means a left-sided lesion. MCA would hit face and arm hardest.

quiz.q: A patient awoke at 07:00 with weakness. He was last seen normal at 22:00 the previous night. What is his last known well time and why does it matter?
choices: 07:00, when symptoms were discovered
22:00, because treatment windows run from the last time he was at baseline
The midpoint between 22:00 and 07:00
It does not matter once imaging is obtained
quiz.why: Last known well is the last moment the patient was verifiably at baseline, so a wake-up deficit may already be hours old. Thrombolysis is generally limited to about 4.5 hours from that moment, with thrombectomy out to 24 hours in selected patients with salvageable penumbra on imaging.

quiz.q: A patient cannot raise the right eyebrow, cannot close the right eye fully, and the right mouth droops. What does the forehead involvement tell you?
choices: The lesion is peripheral, in the facial nerve itself
The lesion is in the left motor cortex
The lesion is in cranial nerve V
The lesion is in the right cerebellum
quiz.why: The forehead receives input from both hemispheres, so a cortical stroke spares it. Loss of forehead movement and eye closure means the facial nerve itself is affected, as in Bell's palsy. CN V carries facial sensation and chewing, not facial expression.

quiz.q: Which cranial nerve, when impaired, causes an inability to abduct the eye and is often the first affected by rising intracranial pressure?
choices: Cranial nerve III
Cranial nerve IV
Cranial nerve VII
Cranial nerve VI
quiz.why: The abducens nerve supplies the lateral rectus and has the longest intracranial course, so it is stretched early as pressure rises. It is called a false localizing sign because it does not indicate where the pressure originates. CN III palsy gives a down-and-out eye with ptosis and a dilated pupil.

quiz.q: A patient sticks out the tongue and it deviates to the left. What does this indicate?
choices: A right hypoglossal nerve lesion
A left facial nerve lesion
A left hypoglossal nerve lesion
A right trigeminal nerve lesion
quiz.why: The tongue deviates toward the weak side, because the intact side pushes it across. So leftward deviation means a left cranial nerve XII problem. CN VII controls facial expression and CN V facial sensation and chewing.

quiz.q: A knife wound hemisects the left side of the cord at T8. Which pattern results below the injury?
choices: Bilateral weakness with intact sensation
Left weakness and left loss of vibration, with right loss of pain and temperature
Right weakness with left loss of pain and temperature
Complete sensory loss with normal strength on both sides
quiz.why: Brown-Sequard syndrome. Corticospinal fibers crossed in the medulla and dorsal columns cross in the medulla too, so both give ipsilateral findings within the cord. The spinothalamic tract crosses within a level or two of entry, so pain and temperature loss appear on the opposite side.

quiz.q: Sensation is intact down to the umbilicus and absent below it. What sensory level is that?
choices: T4
L1
C4
quiz.why: T10 is the umbilicus. T4 is the nipple line, L1 the groin and C4 the top of the shoulders. These six anchors let you assign a sensory level quickly without consulting a full dermatome chart.

quiz.q: A diver with a C5 fracture has BP 82/44, HR 48, and warm, dry, pink skin below the clavicles. What is this and why the bradycardia?
choices: Hemorrhagic shock; the bradycardia is terminal
Spinal shock; reflexes have been lost temporarily
Septic shock; vasodilation from mediators
Neurogenic shock; sympathetic outflow including the cardiac accelerator fibers at T1 to T4 is interrupted
quiz.why: An injury above roughly T6 cuts sympathetic output, so vessels dilate and SVR falls, and because the cardiac accelerator fibers arise at T1 to T4 the heart cannot compensate with tachycardia. Spinal shock describes the flaccid areflexia, not the blood pressure. Hemorrhage must still be excluded in trauma.

quiz.q: A 39-year-old with two days of back pain reports numbness across the buttocks and inner thighs and has been unable to void since yesterday. What is the next step?
choices: Muscle relaxants and outpatient physical therapy
Reassurance, since back pain usually resolves
Urgent imaging and surgical consultation for suspected cauda equina syndrome
Outpatient MRI in two weeks
quiz.why: Saddle anesthesia plus urinary retention is cauda equina syndrome, usually from a large central disc compressing the root bundle below L1. Retention is the most consistent finding, and delay causes permanent bladder and sexual dysfunction, so it is imaged emergently rather than managed conservatively.

quiz.q: Stimulating beta-2 receptors produces which effect?
choices: Vasoconstriction and raised systemic vascular resistance
Bronchodilation
Increased heart rate and contractility
Increased bronchial secretions and bronchoconstriction
quiz.why: One heart, two lungs: beta-1 is cardiac and beta-2 relaxes bronchial and vascular smooth muscle, which is how albuterol opens airways. Alpha-1 constricts vessels, and muscarinic stimulation increases secretions and constricts bronchi.

quiz.q: Two agitated patients arrive with HR 140, BP 178/96, temperature 39 C and dilated pupils. Patient A is drenched in sweat; patient B has hot, dry, flushed skin and has not urinated in 10 hours. What does the difference mean?
choices: A is sympathomimetic and B is anticholinergic
A is anticholinergic and B is sympathomimetic
Both are cholinergic, at different stages
The difference reflects hydration only and has no diagnostic value
quiz.why: Sympathetic innervation of sweat glands uses acetylcholine, so sweating is preserved in stimulant toxicity and blocked in anticholinergic toxicity. The vitals and pupils are identical, so the skin plus urinary retention and absent bowel sounds is what separates them, and it changes the treatment.

quiz.q: A farm worker has drooling, tearing, vomiting, diarrhea, wheezing with copious secretions, miosis and a heart rate of 42. Atropine should be titrated to which endpoint?
choices: A heart rate above 100
Pupil dilation
Resolution of agitation
Drying of bronchial secretions
quiz.why: In cholinergic poisoning the lethal problem is bronchorrhea and bronchospasm, so atropine is dosed until the chest is dry, which can take very large cumulative doses. Heart rate and pupil size are unreliable endpoints. Pralidoxime is added to regenerate acetylcholinesterase.

quiz.q: Why does a single drug, epinephrine, address every component of anaphylaxis?
choices: It blocks histamine release from mast cells directly
It stimulates alpha-1 for vasoconstriction, beta-1 for cardiac support and beta-2 for bronchodilation
It blocks muscarinic receptors, drying secretions
It acts only on beta-2 receptors, and the rest resolves on its own
quiz.why: Anaphylaxis is vasodilation, capillary leak, airway swelling and bronchospasm at once. Epinephrine's alpha-1 activity reverses the vasodilation and reduces mucosal swelling, beta-1 supports the heart, and beta-2 relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. The IM adult dose is 0.3 mg.

quiz.q: A patient opens her eyes to voice, is confused but conversational, and obeys commands. What is her GCS?
quiz.why: Eyes to voice is 3, confused conversation is 4, obeying commands is 6, for a total of 13. Recording the breakdown matters: 13 made of E3 V4 M6 is a very different patient from one who scores 13 with a lower motor component.

quiz.q: How is status epilepticus currently defined?
choices: Five minutes or more of continuous seizure, or repeat seizures without recovery between them
Thirty minutes or more of continuous seizure activity
Any seizure in a patient with no prior history
Any seizure followed by a postictal period longer than one hour
quiz.why: The definition moved to five minutes because seizures that stop on their own nearly always do so within about two minutes, and because excitotoxic neuronal injury plus internalization of GABA receptors begin early, making benzodiazepines progressively less effective the longer treatment is delayed.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient extends and internally rotates both arms to a painful stimulus. What does this posturing indicate?
choices: Decorticate posturing, damage above the midbrain, motor score 3
Normal withdrawal, motor score 4
Localizing, motor score 5
Decerebrate posturing, damage at or below the midbrain, motor score 2
quiz.why: Extension with internal rotation is decerebrate posturing, scored 2, and it reflects damage at or below the midbrain, which carries a worse prognosis than decorticate flexion toward the core, scored 3.

quiz.q: Eight hours after a tibia fracture was casted, a patient requires escalating opioids, screams on passive toe extension, and has a firm swollen calf. Dorsalis pedis pulse is 2+. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Compartment syndrome is excluded by the palpable pulse
This is expected post-injury pain; continue the cast and reassess in the morning
Compartment syndrome is likely, because pulses persist until very late
Deep vein thrombosis, so obtain a duplex ultrasound first
quiz.why: Compartment pressure only needs to exceed capillary perfusion pressure to kill muscle and nerve, which is far below arterial pressure, so pulses remain. Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are the early findings. Waiting for pulselessness means waiting until the limb is lost, and damage begins within 4 to 6 hours.

quiz.q: An 11-year-old has wrist pain after a fall, with tenderness directly over the distal radial growth plate and a normal x-ray. What is the appropriate approach?
choices: Discharge with an elastic bandage, since the film is normal
Treat as a Salter-Harris type I injury with immobilization and orthopedic follow-up
Obtain an MRI before any immobilization
Treat as a wrist sprain with immediate range of motion exercises
quiz.why: A Salter-Harris type I injury runs straight through the physis and frequently shows no radiographic abnormality, because the cartilage is radiolucent and alignment may be preserved. Point tenderness over a physis in a skeletally immature patient is treated as a fracture, since growth arrest can shorten or angle the limb permanently.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a sprain from a strain?
choices: A sprain injures a ligament between bones; a strain injures a muscle or tendon
A sprain injures a tendon; a strain injures a ligament
A sprain involves cartilage; a strain involves bone
The terms are interchangeable
quiz.why: Ligaments connect bone to bone and provide stability, and tearing one is a sprain. Tendons connect muscle to bone and transmit force, and tearing a tendon or muscle is a strain. Both heal slowly because of limited blood supply, and cartilage, having none, does not repair.

quiz.q: A 20-year-old planted her foot and pivoted, heard a pop, and the knee was tense and swollen within 90 minutes. A second patient twisted a loaded knee, has joint line tenderness, catching, and swelling that developed over a full day. What do the effusion timelines suggest?
choices: Both are meniscal tears of differing severity
Both are ACL tears; the timing is incidental
The first is a meniscal tear, the second an ACL tear
The first is an ACL tear with hemarthrosis, the second a meniscal tear
quiz.why: Rapid swelling within hours means blood in the joint, and the ACL is vascular enough to bleed briskly, so a pop with rapid hemarthrosis after a non-contact pivot is an ACL tear (test with Lachman). Meniscal cartilage is largely avascular, so its effusion is reactive synovial fluid accumulating over about a day, with locking and joint line tenderness.

quiz.q: A patient fell on an outstretched hand and has tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox with normal initial radiographs. What is the correct management?
choices: Discharge with a wrist wrap and no follow-up
Range of motion exercises to prevent stiffness
Thumb spica immobilization and repeat or advanced imaging
Immediate operative fixation
quiz.why: Scaphoid fractures are often radiographically occult initially, and the scaphoid's blood supply enters distally, so a missed proximal fracture risks avascular necrosis and nonunion. Snuffbox tenderness is treated as a fracture until repeat films or MRI or CT say otherwise.

quiz.q: An unconscious patient is found on a bathroom floor after an estimated 16 hours, with dark tea-colored urine, diffuse muscle tenderness and a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L. What is the underlying process and the priority?
choices: Acute kidney injury alone; restrict fluids until urine output returns
Rhabdomyolysis; aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation while treating the hyperkalemia
Hemolysis; transfuse packed red cells
Dehydration; give oral rehydration and observe
quiz.why: Prolonged pressure on muscle causes rhabdomyolysis, releasing myoglobin that injures renal tubules along with potassium and phosphate. CK is typically many times normal. Aggressive isotonic fluid is the mainstay, and hyperkalemia is the immediate threat to life. Restricting fluid worsens the renal injury.

scenarios.title: Localizing a stroke from the deficit
scenarios.intro:
This is a reasoning walkthrough, not a treatment drill. You will take one set of described findings and work backward: which side of the brain, which territory, which vessel, and what the clock means.

The case: a 66-year-old right-handed man, brought in by his daughter. She says he was fine at dinner and "went funny" while watching television.

steps.prompt:
On arrival he has a drooping right side of the face, a right arm that falls immediately when lifted, and a right leg that holds against gravity with mild drift. He tries to speak, produces only a few effortful single words, and looks frustrated when he cannot finish a sentence. He follows commands correctly.

Start with side. Which hemisphere?

choices.text: Left hemisphere, because motor pathways cross and the deficit is on the right
choices.feedback: Correct. The corticospinal tract crosses in the medulla, so a right-sided weakness means a left-sided lesion. That he is right-handed matters for the next step, since language is left-sided in roughly 95% of right-handed people.

choices.text: Right hemisphere, because the face droops on the right
choices.feedback: Cortical findings are contralateral, face included. A right facial droop of cortical origin comes from a left hemisphere lesion. The exception to remember is the cerebellum, whose findings stay on the same side.

choices.text: Cannot be determined without imaging
choices.feedback: Imaging will confirm it, but the exam localizes it first, and that is the point of the exercise. Crossed motor pathways and the language findings let you name side and territory at the bedside in under a minute.

steps.prompt:
Now the territory. Compare the limbs: the arm is dense, the face is involved, the leg is nearly spared. And note the language pattern: effortful, sparse output with intact comprehension.

Which vessel does that combination name?

choices.text: Anterior cerebral artery, because the ACA supplies motor cortex
choices.feedback: The ACA does supply motor cortex, but only the medial strip where the leg is mapped. An ACA stroke gives leg weakness worse than arm, often with incontinence and apathy. This patient's leg is the strongest part of him.

choices.text: Middle cerebral artery, because the face and arm occupy the lateral homunculus and Broca's area sits in that territory
choices.feedback: Exactly. The homunculus puts face and hand on the lateral surface, which is MCA, and tucks the leg over the top edge, which is ACA. Effortful speech with preserved comprehension is Broca's aphasia, also MCA territory in the dominant hemisphere.

choices.text: Posterior cerebral artery, because he cannot communicate
choices.feedback: PCA supplies the occipital lobe and thalamus, so its signature is a visual field cut with relatively preserved strength. Nothing here points at vision, and dense arm weakness is not a PCA finding.

choices.text: Basilar artery, because the deficit is severe
choices.feedback: Severity does not localize. Basilar occlusion hits the brainstem and cerebellum, giving the Ds of dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria and dysphagia, crossed findings, and often a depressed level of consciousness. This is a clean lateral-hemisphere picture.

steps.prompt:
His daughter mentions that he also does not seem to notice things on his right. You test and find no neglect; he simply cannot describe what he sees because of the aphasia.

That raises a useful contrast. If this identical motor deficit had occurred with fluent but meaningless speech, or with true neglect of one side, what would that tell you?

choices.text: Fluent meaningless speech points to Wernicke's area in the dominant temporal lobe; true neglect points to a non-dominant parietal lesion
choices.feedback: Right. Both are still MCA territory, but different branches. Broca's is the frontal branch, Wernicke's the temporal branch, and neglect comes from the non-dominant parietal region, which is why left MCA strokes tend to produce aphasia and right MCA strokes produce neglect.

choices.text: Either finding would move the lesion to the cerebellum
choices.feedback: The cerebellum coordinates movement and produces ipsilateral ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor. It does not produce aphasia or neglect, both of which are cortical functions.

choices.text: Either finding would mean the stroke is hemorrhagic rather than ischemic
choices.feedback: The deficit tells you where, not what. Ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes in the same territory produce the same deficits, which is exactly why imaging is required before any thrombolytic decision.

steps.prompt:
The daughter last saw him behaving normally at `19:40`. He is now in front of you at `21:55`. He first appeared unwell to her at about `21:20`, but she was in another room before that.

What is the last known well time, and what does that number decide?

choices.text: 21:20, because that is when the symptoms started
choices.feedback: That is symptom discovery, not last known well. She was out of the room, so the deficit could have begun any time after 19:40. Using the later time would overstate eligibility and risk treating a stroke that is already too old.

choices.text: 19:40, the last moment he was verifiably at baseline, which starts the treatment clock
choices.feedback: Correct, and it puts him about 2 hours 15 minutes out. That is inside the roughly 4.5-hour window for thrombolysis and well inside the thrombectomy window for a large vessel occlusion, which extends to 24 hours in selected patients with imaging evidence of salvageable tissue.

choices.text: The midpoint of the two times, as a reasonable estimate
choices.feedback: Averaging is not a recognized method and it guesses in the direction that increases risk. The convention is deliberately conservative: the last verified normal moment, from a named witness, recorded as a clock time.

steps.prompt:
Last piece, and it is the one that explains why anyone hurries. His CT shows no bleed and no completed large infarct yet, despite an obvious deficit.

Why can the scan look nearly normal while the patient clearly is not?

choices.text: Because the affected tissue is penumbra: stunned below the threshold for function but above the threshold for death, and still salvageable
choices.feedback: That is the whole basis of stroke treatment. The core is already dead, but around it the penumbra is kept marginally alive by collateral flow. It has stopped working, which is what you see on exam, and it dies progressively over hours, which is why reperfusion time is the strongest modifiable predictor of outcome.

choices.text: Because the deficit must be a TIA and will resolve on its own
choices.feedback: A TIA is defined by the absence of infarction on imaging after the symptoms have resolved. These symptoms have not resolved, and a normal early CT is expected in acute ischemia because the changes take hours to appear.

choices.text: Because CT cannot detect a hemorrhage in the first hours
choices.feedback: The opposite is true. CT is excellent at detecting acute blood immediately, which is precisely why it is the first scan: it rules out hemorrhage before any thrombolytic is considered. It is early ischemia that CT shows poorly.

scenarios.debrief:
The method generalizes to any stroke described on paper.

First side: motor and sensory findings are contralateral, so the deficit tells you the opposite hemisphere. The cerebellum is the exception, with ipsilateral ataxia and dysmetria.

Then territory, read off the homunculus. Face and arm worse than leg is MCA. Leg worse than arm is ACA. Visual field loss with preserved strength is PCA. Dizziness travelling with diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia or truncal ataxia is vertebrobasilar.

Then the language and attention findings sort the branch and the dominance. Effortful sparse speech with intact comprehension is Broca's, frontal and dominant. Fluent empty speech without insight is Wernicke's, temporal and dominant. Neglect is non-dominant parietal.

Then the clock. Last known well is the last verified normal moment from a named witness, not when someone noticed. It decides thrombolysis (generally within `4.5 hours`) and thrombectomy (up to `24 hours` in selected large vessel occlusions), and the reason it matters is the penumbra: stunned, silent, salvageable tissue that the core consumes while you wait. And a glucose is checked on every one of these, because hypoglycemia imitates a stroke perfectly.

scenarios.title: Working up a knee
scenarios.intro:
One knee injury, worked the way a clinician does it: mechanism first, then what the exam findings mean, then whether a decision rule applies, then what the structure's blood supply predicts about healing.

The case: a 27-year-old recreational soccer player, seen the evening of the injury.

steps.prompt:
She says she planted her right foot and turned hard to change direction. No one touched her. She felt a pop, the knee gave way, and she could not continue playing. The knee was visibly swollen by the time she reached her car, roughly `45 minutes` later.

Before examining anything, what does the mechanism plus the swelling timeline already suggest?

choices.text: A non-contact pivoting injury with a pop and rapid swelling suggests bleeding inside the joint, which points at a cruciate ligament
choices.feedback: Good reasoning, and it comes from vascularity. Swelling within hours is a hemarthrosis, meaning something with a blood supply tore. The ACL is the classic non-contact pivot injury and bleeds briskly. Meniscal cartilage is largely avascular, so its effusion builds slowly.

choices.text: A meniscal tear, because twisting injuries always involve the meniscus
choices.feedback: Menisci do tear with twisting, usually on a loaded, flexed knee, and they can coexist with an ACL tear. But the timeline argues against it being the main event: meniscal effusions are reactive synovial fluid that accumulate over about a day, not 45 minutes.

choices.text: An MCL tear, because the knee gave way
choices.feedback: Giving way is nonspecific and happens with ligament, meniscal and patellar injuries alike. MCL tears come from a blow to the outside of the knee forcing it inward, and she specifically says no one touched her.

choices.text: A patellar dislocation, since the knee swelled fast
choices.feedback: Patellar dislocation does swell quickly and also follows twisting on a planted foot, so it belongs on the list. But it is usually visibly deformed at the time with the kneecap sitting laterally, and it typically reduces with knee extension, which she would have described.

steps.prompt:
On exam: a tense effusion, the knee held in about `20 degrees` of flexion, and she resists full extension because of pain. There is no bony tenderness over either malleolus, the patella, the fibular head or the tibial tubercle. Distal pulses and sensation are normal.

Which special test is the most sensitive for the structure you suspect, and why is it more sensitive than the alternative?

choices.text: Anterior drawer, because it tests the same ligament at 90 degrees
choices.feedback: It does test the ACL, but at 90 degrees of flexion the hamstrings can guard and the meniscus can block translation, so it is less sensitive, especially in an acute painful knee that will not bend that far.

choices.text: Lachman, tested at about 20 to 30 degrees of flexion, where hamstring guarding is minimal
choices.feedback: Correct. Lachman is performed near the position the knee already prefers, so it is tolerable acutely and less defeated by muscle guarding. It is the most sensitive clinical test for an ACL tear.

choices.text: McMurray, because it is the standard knee test
choices.feedback: McMurray tests the meniscus by rotating a flexed, loaded knee, and it should be done, but it is not the test for the structure the mechanism and timeline point at. Provocative tests also come last in the exam sequence for a reason.

choices.text: Thompson test, squeezing the calf
choices.feedback: Thompson tests Achilles tendon continuity, not the knee. A negative squeeze, meaning no plantar flexion, indicates an Achilles rupture. It belongs to a different injury entirely.

steps.prompt:
Lachman is positive with a soft endpoint. Posterior drawer is negative, there is no laxity on valgus or varus stress, and there is no joint line tenderness today.

She asks whether she needs an x-ray, and points out that her ankle also hurts a little from landing. The ankle has no malleolar or midfoot bone tenderness, and she walked four steps in the room without help.

How do you handle imaging?

choices.text: X-ray both the knee and the ankle, since any injured joint should be imaged
choices.feedback: Imaging everything is not neutral: it adds radiation, time and cost, and it does not make a ligament injury visible. Validated decision rules exist precisely so that low-risk joints can be cleared clinically.

choices.text: No ankle x-ray, because the Ottawa ankle rules are satisfied; knee imaging is a separate judgment and will not show the ligament anyway
choices.feedback: Right on both halves. Ottawa requires bone tenderness at a malleolus, the fifth metatarsal base or the navicular, or an inability to take four steps, and she has none of those; applied properly the rules approach 100% sensitivity for clinically significant fractures. And an x-ray cannot show an ACL, which is why the diagnosis is clinical with MRI for confirmation.

choices.text: Skip all imaging permanently, since ligaments do not appear on x-ray
choices.feedback: Half right in a way that could cost you. Films do not show ligaments, but they do show the fractures that accompany these mechanisms, such as a Segond avulsion or a tibial plateau fracture, and knee decision rules exist for exactly that question.

choices.text: Order an MRI tonight before doing anything else
choices.feedback: MRI will eventually confirm the tear and any associated meniscal injury, but it is not an emergency study for a neurovascularly intact knee. The acute questions are fracture, neurovascular status and stability, all answerable at the bedside.

steps.prompt:
You reassess the whole limb before she leaves: skin intact, compartments soft, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 2+, sensation normal on the dorsum and sole, and she can wiggle her toes.

Why is this step documented specifically, and what would change your plan?

choices.text: Because a documented pre-splint neurovascular exam is the only way to show a later deficit was not caused by the splint, and a hard, tense, exquisitely painful compartment would change everything
choices.feedback: Exactly. Neurovascular status is recorded before and after every splint or reduction. And the specific thing you are screening for is compartment syndrome, whose early signs are pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch, long before pulses disappear.

choices.text: Because it is a formality that rarely changes management
choices.feedback: It changes management in exactly the cases you cannot afford to miss. A knee dislocation, which can spontaneously reduce and look like a bad sprain, threatens the popliteal artery, and compartment syndrome in the leg develops over hours.

choices.text: Because absent pulses are the earliest sign of compartment syndrome
choices.feedback: Pulselessness is one of the five Ps but it is late and unreliable, because compartment pressure only has to exceed capillary perfusion pressure to kill muscle. The early findings are pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch.

steps.prompt:
She asks why this will take months when the sprained ankle she had last year was fine in three weeks.

Answer her with tissue biology.

choices.text: Because ligaments have a poor blood supply compared with bone, and the intra-articular ACL heals particularly badly, which is why reconstruction is often needed
choices.feedback: That is the right level of explanation. Bone is richly vascular and remodels, uniting in roughly 6 weeks in the upper limb and 12 or more in the lower. Ligaments and tendons are far less vascular and heal slowly, and the ACL sits bathed in joint fluid where a torn end cannot form a useful clot.

choices.text: Because ligaments are made of the same tissue as cartilage and never heal at all
choices.feedback: Close but wrong in a way that matters. Cartilage is avascular and essentially does not repair. Ligaments are dense collagen with a limited blood supply, so they do heal, just slowly, and many extra-articular ones such as the MCL heal well without surgery.

choices.text: Because the swelling itself is what delays healing, so it will resolve as soon as the effusion is drained
choices.feedback: Aspirating a tense hemarthrosis can relieve pain, but the effusion is a consequence of the tear, not the cause of slow healing. Removing fluid does not restore a torn ligament's continuity or its blood supply.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to carry out of this case is that mechanism plus effusion timing plus one good special test usually names the structure before any imaging.

Mechanism sorts the list. Non-contact pivot and deceleration points at the ACL. A dashboard blow driving the tibia backward points at the PCL. A blow to the outside of the knee points at the MCL. Twisting on a loaded, flexed knee points at the meniscus.

Effusion timing reads vascularity. Blood within hours means something vascular tore, most often the ACL. Fluid over a day is reactive and fits a meniscal injury, because meniscal cartilage is largely avascular.

The tests each have a reason. Lachman beats anterior drawer because it is performed at `20` to `30 degrees`, where the hamstrings cannot guard. McMurray loads and rotates the meniscus. Thompson checks Achilles continuity. Valgus and varus stress isolate the collateral ligaments.

Decision rules replace habit with evidence. The Ottawa ankle rules image only for bone tenderness at a malleolus, the fifth metatarsal base or the navicular, or an inability to take four steps, and they are close to `100%` sensitive for significant fractures.

And the exam sequence never changes: inspection, palpation, active then passive range of motion, strength `0` to `5`, neurovascular check, and provocative special tests last. The neurovascular check is documented before and after every splint.
